speechtext:
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, I wish to raise a question of privilege of which I gave you notice earlier this morning.
I was surprised this morning when listening to the CBC Radio-News to learn that three Members of Parliament, the Member for Megantic-Compton-Stanstead (Mr. Gerin), the Member for Richelieu (Mr. Plamondon), and the Member for Charlevoix (Mr. Hamelin) had received and made comment on a Bill not yet tabled in the House and therefore not available to all Members of Parliament for similar comment. I refer to a Bill to amend the Official Languages Act.
I would like from you clarification on this practice. It is my recollection that it is against the rules and customs of the House for the Government to make available to one group of Members a Bill for comment that is not made available to others. I think that requires some clarification and direction on your part.
I can understand the Government discussing the principles of a Bill that it will table with some Members of Parliament, including its own caucus, but not giving those Members the final Bill for comment publicly. I can also understand the Government providing Bills and documents to the official critics in the Opposition, but again under the obligation that they shall not make those Bills or proposals public, and not comment on them until the Bill has been tabled in the House.
In this case, the Member for Charlevoix said that according to the Bill Anglo-Quebecers would have no reason to worry. Perhaps he is right, but I, as a Member representing a Quebec riding with a majority of Anglophones, have no way of responding or commenting on his comments.
I would appreciate your clarification on this rule and custom of the House. If you feel that 1 have a prima facie case of privilege I will move that the matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedures.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present, in both official languages, the fourth report the Standing Joint Committee on Official Languages.

Pursuant to Standing Order 99(2) of the House of Commons, the committee asks the Government to table a response to this report within 150 days.

The report makes recommendation for necessary changes to official languages policy and programs within the federal jurisdiction as a result of testimony received from 16 government departments and agencies.

The committee firmly believes the Treasury Board must play to a greater degree its key role in the co-ordination of official languages programs for the whole Public Service, and it recommends that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Mazankowski) present Parliament with a report on the status of official languages at the time the Main Estimates are tabled.
The committee further recommends that a plan regarding official languages be submitted each year by all federal departments and agencies to the Treasury Board.

Also included are recommendations that the minimum language knowledge level of positions offering a service to the public be eliminated in favour of an intermediate knowledge level and that managers and supervisors be required to possess a superior knowledge of the second official language.

Finally, the report recommends an efficient control system be established for the payment of the bilingualism bonus.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I very much welcome this opportunity to participate in the capital punishment debate. I support the re-establishment of capital punishment in Canada. However, I think it would be worthwhile to narrow the issues we are discussing today to those contained in the motion.
In order to bring about focus on the real issues, let me start by disposing of some of the arguments which have received some attention thus far in the debate.
It is often asserted that before capital punishment was officially eliminated in 1976 the law had ceased to be effective and, therefore, restoring the status quo ante-1976 will accomplish nothing. Let me state that I agree with this argument.
The second emotive argument which is raised is that somehow those of us who wish to reinstate capital punishment want to bring back the noose. This is not what I want, nor what the vast majority of Canadians want.
The third argument which is raised is that society has progressed beyond the "eye for an eye" mentality; that is, that
June 25, 1987

vengeance should not be the principal thrust of a modern judicial system. I also agree with this concept, as do the vast majority of MPs and the public.
The fourth argument which is raised is that if capital punishment is reinstated it will become more difficult to convict murderers. I personally consider this a strong argument in favour of the reinstatement of capital punishment. The implicit assumption underlying it is that somehow jurors are convicting people of murder now notwithstanding that they have genuine doubt as to guilt. With capital punishment in place, jurors would be more reluctant to convict in the absence of resolving all doubt.
I personally feel that juries should not be handing down guilty verdicts in circumstances where they have some doubt as to guilt. If the availability of capital punishment will cause jurors to take the extra time for consideration before bringing in a guilty verdict, I would consider that to be an argument in favour of the reinstatement of capital punishment.
The question then which is relevant to the capital punishment debate is this. Does one favour taking a human life under any circumstances and, if so, on what basis? If so, the matter of which crimes should be potentially subject to capital punishment and who should impose the sentence, as well as the method of execution to be used, must also be considered.
When I first entered politics nine years ago I decided it would be prudent to ask myself, in the privacy of my own home, what my beliefs and convictions were, so that when I appeared in a public forum or gave interviews to the press, I would not be left to wing it; that rather, I would have a comprehensive philosophical and political basis on which to respond.
I must admit that until I sat down and wrote a list of the questions that I could be asked, I had not given the issue of capital punishment much time or thought. What thought I had given it led me to believe that capital punishment should not be imposed in the majority of first degree murder cases, since most first degree murders were committed by close family members, and murderers falling into this category show a remarkable degree of rehabilitation. Nor did I believe that an accomplice who was waiting in the get-away vehicle should be equally liable for the death penalty as the person who went into a bank and shot a teller.
However, as I considered that decision, my mind turned to individuals such as those who killed the Portuguese shoe-shine boy, Emanuel Jaques. After holding the boy for several days and assaulting him, they then drowned him.
I also began to think of cases involving young children, particularly girls, who were murdered following violent rape or sexual molestation, as well as, of course, serial killers, of whom there are all too many, who principally abduct, assault and kill young women.
In these situations, it seems to me that there is a valid case for capital punishment. The rationale, of course, is primarily
Capital Punishment
one of public safety, although there is a substantial element of deterrence. For example, questions asked of the killers of Emanuel Jaques elicited the response that had there been capital punishment, they would not likely have proceeded to kill the boy. Similarly, there are examples of lifers, particularly those guilty of multiple murders, who have nothing to lose in trying to escape and as a consequence inflict serious or deadly assaults upon prison guards.
In these situations of serial murders and murders which involve rape or child assault, in the case of murders involving any violent crime, or in the case of murders done for ideological reasons, particularly the so-called executions of innocent hostages, I found, in closely examining myself, that I believed the public safety was best served by reinstating capital punishment. Having reached this conclusion, the questions were these. What sort of system should be brought into being, how would this differ from the old system, and how could a structure best be set up to achieve the desired results?
Over the last nine years I have had many discussions with constituents and participated in well over 100 all-candidate debates in which the issue of capital punishment has often arisen. By and large I found that most of the population had not thought out the issue thoroughly. They tended initially to engage in a knee-jerk reaction to the issue. However, after prolonged discussions, I found that the vast majority of Canadians seem to have similar views to my own.
With this in mind, I ran a referendum in my riding early this year. In my referendum I did not simply ask a black and white question such as, "Are you in favour of capital punishment?" I took steps to explain the issues to my constituents and to use open-ended questions to seek their views.
I indicated that I would treat the referendum seriously, that I genuinely desired to know the views of my constituents, and that I would reflect their thinking in my speech in the House of Commons.
The response was overwhelming. Over 16,300 ballots were returned; by far the largest response ever received by any Member of Parliament on any issue up to that time. About 10 per cent of these ballots either included lengthy comments in the section provided on the ballot or contained letters. The ballot of course was conducted completely anonymously, but many individuals took the opportunity to sign their names to the letters.
I was interested to find out that my constituents' views closely coincided with my own. First, there was no support whatsoever for an automatic death sentence for any crime. However, the vast majority of my constituents believe that capital punishment can be justified under one or more circumstances.
Almost two-thirds of the respondents felt that capital punishment should potentially be available to any person who

commits first degree murder. Almost one-quarter of respondents feel that this is too widespread and that capital punishment should only be potentially available for some first degree murders. Of this minority, more than three-quarters cited murders of police and jail guards, and just over one-half cited murder in the act of committing another violent crime as potential capital offences.
However, the psyche of my constituents was much more interestingly revealed in respect of a question about serious terrorist acts which did not involve taking a human life. The hypothetical example I cited was drawn from real life and dealt with a terrorist who intended to blow up an airliner by planting a bomb in the hand luggage of his fiance. The fact that he did not succeed in committing murder was not due to his efforts but due to the diligence of the airline inspection system. Astoundingly, more people favour capital punishment for terrorism of this type even though no life was taken than favour capital punishment for first degree murder.
These results and many notes and letters which I received indicated quite clearly that the public's desire to see capital punishment reinstated was first and foremost based on a concern for public safety. Some people who have committed the vilest and most violent type of murder were judged simply too dangerous to have around. In addition, there was and is a steely determination to take whatever steps are necessary to ensure that the type of terrorism against innocent people now prevalent in Europe or in the Middle East does not spread to Canada. It was for these reasons that people overwhelmingly supported the resurrection of the death penalty.
The second question I asked was, "Who should impose the sentence"? Once again the public's view coincided closely with my own and represented a complete rejection of the previous system. The public simply does not want the very serious decision to take a life to rest in the hands of any one individual such as the judge. Over 85 per cent of the respondents felt that the jury should first vote whether the individual was guilty or innocent of a potentially capital offence and then, immediately after returning this decision, the jury should be asked for its recommendation on whether the sentence should be a capital one. Some 27 per cent of respondents felt that the jury alone should be society's surrogates and should determine whether capital punishment is imposed, while over 58 per cent felt the jury should express its opinion to the judge directly and that the judge should bear its views in mind before imposing the sentence.
It is quite clear that the public does not wish to delegate this authority to any one individual who may be a so-called "hanging judge" that automatically imposes the sentence or who may have, on the other hand, a philosophical opposition to imposing capital punishment. The public wants any decision to take a life to be based on an extremely wide forum-those jurors who have heard all the evidence.
I was very interested to learn that such a double jury vote system exists in other parts of the world and that in practice
results very similar to those I intuitively felt should be obtained were obtained. Only rarely is capital punishment imposed in cases of murder involving close family members, the area with the greatest likelihood of rehabilitation. However, for serial killers, killers of hostages, and killers caught in the act of committing another crime such as rape or child molestation, the death penalty is frequently imposed.
Finally, I asked what method of execution should be selected. The restitution of the noose received only 9 per cent support. Overwhelmingly, by their votes and in their comments, people indicated that if they found the taking of a human life necessary, it should only be done in the most humane method possible.
Older people of both sexes, particularly those likely to have encountered serious operations, strongly supported lethal injection. They, as I, have experience with general anaesthesia and know that within 20 seconds a person can be rendered unconscious and that a lethal injection can then be administered.
Younger voters were more apt to favour allowing the condemned to have the choice. However, once again they clearly indicated that they desired the most humane method possible. Consistently, almost three-quarters of the respondents chose these two options for both sexes and at all ages. The public does not believe in an "eye for an eye" or in revenge, and neither do I. If the deed is to be done, we want it to be done using the most humane method possible.
Some people might believe that capital punishment is in some way playing God and no one has the right to decide when a life should be taken, that this is a decision that should be left to God. Certainly I respect this view, and the more consistently it is espoused, the more respect I have for it. The people who are most consistent in terms of this view are those who in wartime are conscientious objectors even when the fabric of society itself is threatened.
For example, even with Hitler threatening in the Second World War, these people were consistent and refused to accept that taking a life could be justified by bearing arms. I have the highest respect for those who hold this view. However, I do not share it. I believe society can justify taking a life when public safety is involved.
When society has identified individuals who pose such a threat to public safety, who have committed crimes such as serial killing or murders after torture or brutalization, society, in the form of the jury, has the right to judge that they represent a threat to society's safety and that society has the right to protect itself by taking a human life.
In my mind there is no consistent philosophical basis for accepting the right to take a life in defence of one's country because public safety is threatened or self-defence is threatened, and yet hold out the philosophical argument that taking a life can never be justified.
June 25, 1987

The vast majority of Canadians feel that when individual or public safety is threatened, killing of individuals in self-defence or through declaration of war is justified. It is my contention that the views of society in respect of capital punishment have exactly the same philosophical basis of the right to public safety, and it is for this reason that they and I support the reinstatement of capital punishment.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REINSTATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in the House of Commons to speak to my fellow Members of Parliament and to my constituents, many of whom have written to me here in Ottawa, have called me, have spoken with me on the streets in Vancouver-Kingsway, or have met me on the doorsteps of their houses.
I want to begin by saying that on this extremely complex moral issue 1 owe my constituents my own judgment. This is in accordance with a long parliamentary tradition going back to the British Member of Parliament, Edmund Burke, who, speaking to the electors of Bristol on November 13, 1774, said:
Your representative owes you, not his industry alone, but his judgment, and he betrays instead of serving you if he sacrifices it to your opinion.
While my own Party has a policy on capital punishment, I am here exercising my own judgment on this issue. That is not to say that I do not respect or consider the views of my constituents, or indeed the views of other Members like the one who has just spoken, who take a view different from the one I take. I have read their letters carefully and I have listened to their views carefully and sincerely, and I respect them all.
This debate is really a life and death debate. If we restore capital punishment, people will be executed by the state. It would be foolish to assume otherwise. That is why I take this debate very seriously.
I am concerned that many Canadians may think there is an easy way for the state to kill, in a sanitized way, if you like. The Hon. Member who just spoke talked about lethal injections. Maybe we will not have the noose, the electric chair or the kind of circus atmosphere that accompanies American state executions, but I remind Canadians and fellow Members that the state will be taking the life of a fellow human being whether it be in a sanitized way through the lethal injection or through a more public and circus like way of the noose or the electric chair.
Members of Parliament all have different ways of coming at this question. In the period before I entered the House of Commons, I practised criminal law. I think I have the unique situation among Members of this House that as a former Crown attorney and former defence counsel I prosecuted someone charged with murder and I defended someone charged with murder. I will never forget-it is one of these incidents that stands out in one's memory-the murder case that I handled in Prince Rupert when I was a young lawyer. It was my first murder case and I defended a young native woman who was charged with murdering her husband.
Capital Punishment
I practised law in a period in which the death penalty was abolished but I recall the older lawyers telling me how often juries would refuse to convict even in fairly strong cases because they could see the accused before them. They knew that they were personally sentencing a human being to death. In many cases they simply could not do this. Often people who normally would have been convicted were acquitted, and studies bear this out. To me, this is a more accurate reflection of the real views of the ordinary Canadian than the mere answering of a phone call from a polling organization.
During my practice as a criminal lawyer I came to have a deep respect for our criminal justice system. I think it is one of the best and the fairest in the world. I also saw first hand, because it is a system that functions through human beings, that mistakes can happen. When the state hangs an innocent person, and that has happened in the United States, in Britain and perhaps in Canada, there is no correcting that mistake. You cannot bring the person back. Indeed, along with other kinds of sentences, I feel the application of the death penalty will be, and has been, discriminatory and will fall on those least able to get a good lawyer, the poor, the under-educated, the inarticulate, the mentally retarded, the emotionally disturbed and minorities, and studies in the United States bear this out.
As a criminal lawyer, I also got the opportunity to see criminals as human beings, often pathetic, desperate, sometimes sick human beings, usually inadequate in some way, people who did not fit into society and people who belonged to a minority. More often than not they were poor. That is why I am not surprised to find that studies clearly show that capital punishment is no deterrent to murder.
Why then, I ask myself, this demand to restore capital punishment, given that there has been no real change in murder rates since we abolished the death penalty. Is it a religious demand? The Christian Bible says in the Old Testament, "Thou shalt not kill. An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, a hand for a hand, a foot for a foot". But Jesus of Nazareth in the Bible says:
Ye have heard that it hath been said, 'An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth' but I say unto you, that ye resist no evil: But whoever shall smite thee on thy cheek, turn to him the other also.
Most churches have written to me against the death penalty. In 1983 the Pope himself spoke out against capital punishment. Therefore, I do not think the argument for the return of the death penalty is based on religious grounds.
I have a letter from a woman whose daughter was murdered. She tells us that capital punishment will not bring back her daughter; nor indeed, even if restored, will it deter murders of other daughters. Unfortunately, that will be a fact of life.
Why then the demand for restoration of capital punishment, Mr. Speaker? I think it is based on revenge, which is still a natural part of the human make-up, a part that we still have not yet conquered, together with the frustrations of modern life which come from the feeling that in the modern world we

June 25, 1987
Capital Punishment
cannot control what goes on in our lives. The Hon. Member who spoke last spoke of terrorism. Capital punishment is still, and really is, state vengeance and I think it comes down to being part of our penal philosophy. To restore capital punishment abandons hope in our ability to cope with violence, whether it be criminal or otherwise, except with more violence.
John Donne, the great English poet, many years ago said:
Any man's death diminishes me because I am involved in mankind.
I conclude that to restore the death penalty no matter how it is done would be a step backward for Canada. It would place us among the more barbaric and violent states of the world. The death penalty is out of place in a modern, peaceful, humane society, which is my vision of Canada. Therefore, I will vote against the motion.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REINSTATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to speak, not only to those who, like myself, are against a return to capital punishment but especially to those who today still believe that reinstatement of this ultimate penalty is truly justified.
During the few minutes I am allowed, I would like to explain my reasons for opposing capital punishment today, as I did in 1976.
Before I go any further, I would like to express very briefly my profound dismay, which I am sure is shared by many of my colleagues, at the way the Government put this question before the House and the way it intends to conduct the debate.
During the last election campaign, the Prime Minister promised Canadians that once elected, his Government would hold a free vote on capital punishment. We thought this would involve a clear and straight forward process and that the House would decide the issue with all the moral and political consequences that would entail, both for the individual Member and for the Government.
Instead, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Government have decided to play hide and seek. They have decided to hide their true colours behind a quite perilous procedure, considering the nature of the debate and what is at stake.
On tabling his motion in the House on February 13 this year, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) said the tabling of the motion did not mean the Government approved or disapproved of reinstating capital punishment.
However, the motion he tabled on behalf of the Government and on which we will be asked to vote is crystal-clear in this respect, and I quote:
That this House supports, in principle, the reinstatement of capital punishment-
And the Government would have us believe it is not taking sides!
This manoeuvre would let the Government take its distance from a debate that will not enhance any reputations or produce any winners.
I suggest we take a closer look at the content of the motion. Briefly, the motion tabled by the Deputy Prime Minister asks the House to support reinstatement of capital punishment and orders the appointment of a special committee consisting of 15 members, a committee that is to hold hearings for three months across the country and make recommendations, on the basis of the testimony received, regarding:
(1)	the offences that should carry the death penalty;
(2)	the methods by which the sentence should be carried out; and finally,
(3)	the same committee will be responsible for preparing and bringing in a Bill.
We have here the three basic elements of what normally should have been the Government's responsibility: the crimes that should be punishable by capital punishment, the methods used and the requisite drafting of legislation.
Mr. Speaker, when the previous Liberal Government tabled Bill C-84 in 1976, it did so frankly and forthrightly. It did not seek every kind of excuse to shirk its reponsibilities. It fully recognized its responsibilities, and it did so after a free vote in which the Prime Minister at the time and his Cabinet voted in favour of Bill C-84, to adopt the motion taking capital punishment out of the Criminal Code.
This Government is trying to to eat its cake and have it too. Government Members are divided on the issue, that we know. The Cabinet seems to be as well. And so they do not want to have the responsibility for this motion. Once the debate is concluded, they want to be able to tell proponents of capital punishment that they kept their word. They want to be able to tell the others, the people who are against capital punishment: Well, what can we do? The decision was made by a committee of the House with Members from all three Parties.
The motion is a highly regrettable one. I am also concerned that some Members, instead of acting as responsible Members, prefer to bow to the majority views of some Canadians. Members who want to shirk their responsibilities tell us: in the final instance, it doesn't really matter whether I'm for or against capital punishment since the majority of my constituents are in favour, and that is why I intend to vote for the motion.
Personally, I think that in the final instance, a Member should be accountable for his actions to his constituents. I believe a Member must answer for his actions to the people who elected him, but this does not imply that he can shirk that same political responsibility by giving up his freedom to speak, and especially his freedom to think and his freedom to vote in this House. Were he to act this way, I do not think he would be doing a service to his constituents, nor would he be enhancing
June 25, 1987

the quality of our system of Government, and indeed the quality of our democratic life.
This debate borders on the realm of unreality for those who, like myself, had the privilege of being here when Parliament voted to abolish capital punishment in 1976, convinced as we were at the time that, after a long and difficult debate, our country had finished a very significant and historic journey.
We thought at the time that as parliamentarians and, more fundamentally, as Canadians, we had turned a page of our collective history. We thought that we had clearly signified to the world our deep commitment to human values. We thought that we had signified our commitment to justice and to life in voting for the abolition of the death penalty. We thought that we had expressed in 1976, collectively and individually, our fundamental belief in the primacy of human life, and that in doing so we had joined the family of enlightened peoples.

So we are wondering today how we ever got to the point where again we would want to change everything and move backwards.
Admittedly our country has been witness to sordid crimes in recent years, often involving children. Our television screens at home have often shown scenes of horror and suffering.
The same television has enabled us to see-and feel, to a certain extent-the sufferings of parents who had just lost a child, or the sufferings of a wife who had just lost her policeman husband coldly shot dead while on duty. Undoubtedly such incidents have stirred emotions and raised fear and indignation among many Canadians.

But that same television has also magnified tenfold the tales of human suffering. It has magnified our horror and indignation by feeding us a steady diet of violent programming. Indeed, every night on prime time, we see murder, robbery, assault, rape and kidnapping. Unfortunately, very often these are American programs.
All of this makes us believe that somehow we have in the last 10 years changed fundamentally as a society and become more violent, more brutal than we were when we had the death penalty. I think this is not the real fact. Rather than numbing us to the real violence, it makes us feel weak and defenceless and leads us to believe that our penal system is faulty, that we need to protect ourselves because the state no longer can protect us from a violence which is nevertheless more often perceived than real. We began to advocate capital punishment, and as things went on some Conservative Members of Parliament decided to press on, and here now we have the Government presenting a motion to reinstate capital punishment. I think this is a very sad situation.
Capital Punishment

I am very sincere when I suggest that the quality of our judicial system will not be enhanced if we vote to restore capital punishment. Nor will it be an accomplishment for those who advocate the repeal of the existing statute in favour of the reinstatement of the death penalty. A man like Clifford Olson will be the real winner because he will thus bring us down to his own lowly common denominator. As I see it, such a move would make our society less humane from the outset, and we will certainly be less tolerant, less avid of freedom.
In conclusion, I should like to quote from a statement released by the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops entitled "The Escalation of Violence", which I recommend to all my colleagues:
A society which so respects the right to life that it cannot resort to capital punishment to protect itself creates an atmosphere which commands respect for other human rights. The death penalty is acceptable only in a society which is not well organized enough to find another way to defend itself against elements which would threaten the lifes of its citizens, and such is not the case in Canada. Violence begets violence, and capital punishment is a violent measure. Today still, ten years after capital punishment was abolished, we harbour the same conviction: a society which respects the sacred and intangible character of human life and which gives top priority to human rights definitely promotes its own social progress, even though this may seem to be a slow and not immediately apparent process, besides contributing to the development of mankind. This conviction, confirmed in the message of Jean-Paul II when he visited our country, is based on the evangelical project where guilty mankind is reconciled with God thanks to the pardon of Jesus. Innocent, but convicted and sentenced to death, Jesus himself advocates total forgiveness: "Forgive them, Father, for they do not know what they are doing."
I think we can admit that a society such as ours has the right to punish a criminal, the right to inflict a sanction which is proportional to the crime, but I maintain that killing a man to punish him is tantamount to vengeange, and nothing else.
In this respect, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote former Prime Minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau:
As members of society, do we have so little respect for ourselves, so little hope of bettering human condition, are we so near social bankruptcy that we accept the principle of State vengeance as the cornerstone of our penal philosophy?
Finally, I would ask all Members in this House, whether you support or oppose reinstating capital punishment, to vote according to your conscience. Discuss this with your constituents, of course, discuss it also with your families, but by all means do not vote because a majority of voters in your constituency want capital punishment back, and want society to be brought back to a state of barbary. On the contrary, vote according to your conscience, and above all vote in a manner where liberty will prevail, rather than vengeance.

Mr. Speaker, I have two short observations to make and a question to ask of the Hon. Member.

June 25, 1987
Capital Punishment
Tie referred to the 1976 vote and how he thought that would resolve the issue for all time. I beg to differ. If that vote had reflected the wish of the majority of the Canadian people, I suggest it might have helped resolve the problem. However, we had a so-called free vote in 1976, and he knows as well as anyone in this country that there was a solid cabinet vote opposing the retention of capital punishment. Yet many of the cabinet Ministers in that Liberal Government spoke out in support of capital punishment prior to the vote.
We have today a parallel with 1976. According to a recent Maclean's magazine poll, 68 per cent of members of the PC Party support capital punishment in one form or other; in the Liberal Party it is 61 per cent, and in the NDP it is 55 per cent. If the Government and elected representatives in Parliament ignore the vast majority who support capital punishment, the same thing will happen as happened in 1976.
How does the Hon. Member propose to deal with this desire of the Canadian people; by ignoring them time after time after time? How does he expect the issue to ever go away if Parliament does not pay at least some attention to the majority?

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REINSTATEMENT
speechtext:
I am pleased to respond to the Hon. Member by reminding him that capital punishment was abolished in Canada in 1976 by the Canadian Parliament, with the knowledge that such was basically the case in most western- industrialized nations- France, Belgium, Britain and so forth, and at the time Canadian parliamentarians wanted thereby to ensure that we express our deep respect for human rights, and what we did in fact was put an end to an experience that dated back to barbaric, archaic customs.
The fact was that both the then Liberal Government and the previous Conservative Government had refused to hang those who had been sentenced to death. It will be remembered that in a systematic way, both the Diefenbaker Government and the Pearson Government, as well as the Trudeau Government, when a death sentence was sent to Cabinet for commuting to life imprisonment, those successive Cabinets in a systematic way commuted all death sentences to life imprisonment.
The reality therefore in Canada was that already the Government, inspired by that modern spirit of treating prisoners, criminals in a modern rather than archaic way, had decided no longer to hang criminals.
The legislation passed by Parliament in 1976 was therefore confirming a tradition that had been well anchored into Canadian usage by various Cabinets, both Liberal and Conservative.
Capital punishment proved a punitive act rather than a reforming move. Clearly, those who claim that capital punishment will prevent a criminal from killing are mistaken. It never was and never will be a rehabilitating action, a sentence that will bring someone, with the thought that if he goes ahead and kills someone he will be hanged, along the
road, to decide not to commit his crime, knowing he will be hanged. Reality is quite different.
Therefore, we are assuming it would be much more important to have a correctional and judicial system based on administrative reform and a more modern way of operating our judicial system, than going backwards with that punitive form that in my view should have no place in modern society.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether the Hon. Member listened to my speech a while ago, but I clearly indicated that there is a fundamental difference in approach between the steps taken in 1976 and those of the current Government.
Walking both sides of the fence at once, this Conservative Government is trying to keep everybody happy. While some are for abolishing capital punishment, others insist on reinstating it. So, instead of moving a clear and definite motion, it uses this shaw of creating a parliamentary committee.
In 1976, with the support of his full Cabinet, the Prime Minister of the time had opted for abolishing capital punishment, and the motion moved by the Government of the time had made it possible for all Hon. Members from both sides of the House to vote freely on this issue.
But the Government, I mean the Prime Minister and his Ministers were all of the same view, namely, that the time had come to end this barbarous practice and abolish capital punishment. All back-benchers had an opportunity to vote according to their conscience.
I must say that some of my hon. colleagues did not try to justify their position with Gallup or other polls. They voted clearly for or against abolishing capital punishment. It was a free vote. Quite evidently, the Liberal Cabinet of the day was fully behind abolishing capital punishment and so was the Prime Minister. It is a clear situation which does not exist now, something I deplore enormously.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REINSTATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is certainly a privilege for me to rise in this House on this most important debate, perhaps one of the most important, talked
June 25, 1987

about, controversial, and possibly agonizing debates that we have had in this Parliament. This debate deserves the full attention of this House. No matter what side a Member may take on this issue, this is indeed an ultimate test for each Member in decision-making. We might even ask for the wisdom of Solomon to help us make a decision.
In making a decision none is 100 per cent right. We may be 80 per cent or 90 per cent right, and that is how decisions are made. We have to make our decisions reflecting generally the views of our constituents. We are talking about whether we oppose or support capital punishment.
The views of each Member will, of course, be at odds with those of some constituents, because in every constituency there will be a certain number of people in favour and a certain number against. How can a Member of Parliament reflect everyone's view? This is the decision that we as parliamentarians have to take in order to reflect what we, in our wisdom, after consultation not only with our constituents but with other Members of Parliament and groups of people, believe is in the best interests of the people of Canada.
This issue appeals to emotion as well as logic. Hopefully we will not rely on emotions only. We must use our hearts and our minds and they must always be open to the arguments, thoughts and beliefs of others. We must make our decision with care, thought and responsibility.
I will be voting in favour of the reinstatement of capital punishment. I would like to explain to you why I believe that capital punishment should be reinstated in Canada. I believe that the state not only has the right but the responsibility to protect itself and its citizens from harm. We are waging a war of sorts against crime in its most barbarous form, that is, murder in first degree, the taking of innocent lives. We as a state must protect our citizens from those who would seek to destroy life within our country.
If a foreign country were to invade our borders we; individuals, soldiers, sailors, men and women, would not hesitate to fight back, to punish the invaders, especially those who may have killed our citizens in the process of the invasion. By fighting back we would most likely take the lives of the invaders. This is the role of the state to protect its inhabitants. It must provide a safe haven for its citizens. In a way, to kill the invaders is capital punishment and is part of the protection which the state must provide. It must punish the enemy for having taken a life within our country.
Within Canada the enemy is the individual who deliberately plans and kills innocent members of our society. The state must have the power to exercise its strength as protector and must have within its jurisdiction the power to choose the ultimate punishment for the ultimate crime, for example, that of murder in the first degree or high treason.
Canadian citizens are starting to live in fear in their own homes. Seniors are frightened to walk alone at night. Many people expect us to accept that as part of the changing times,
Capital Punishment
part of the 80s and 90s-the reality of life. Well, this is not right and we must not stand for it. Canadians should feel safe, not only in their own homes but throughout the country. It is up to us as legislators to ensure that safety, with our police forces and other protectionist forces.
We must become more sensitive to the rights of victims. They did not choose to become victims but were chosen by the perpetrators of violent crimes. Many people have forfeited their lives in senseless, brutal murders. It is becoming obvious that the state is not responding to their basic need and want, that being to live a safe and secure life.
I share the same view as the majority of my constituents. Last year I conducted a survey of my constituents to learn their views on the issue of capital punishment. At that time 81 per cent supported the return of capital punishment for first degree murder and the murder of police and prison guards. The majority of comments which I read in the questionnaires expressed fear and outrage at the tragedy which befell the victims. They also expressed the perception that our judicial system was possibly somewhat impotent.
In my town hall meetings I have heard many views on the issue of capital punishment. I have never hesitated to ask those who have gathered for their thoughts. The general view that I hear again and again is that the judicial system is not working in favour of law-abiding citizens but rather against them and that we should have capital punishment. The ratio is usually three or four to one in favour of capital punishment.
I have had conversations with members of the clergy who have supported the reinstatement of the death penalty. When I visit community groups and schools and knock on the doors of my constituents I invariably ask them what they think of capital punishment. The views I hear reinforce my belief. Not everyone is in favour of capital punishment, but the vast majority is.
In one high school which I visited this spring we talked of many things including capital punishment. When I asked for a straw vote the result was two to one in favour of capital punishment, this from 16 and 17-year old students.
People do not want to live their lives in fear. It is not a prevailing fear but rather a sense of disquiet that all is not quite right. Part of this disquiet comes from the fact that men and women who have not been rehabilitated are roaming the streets. At a time when the quality of our lives should be at its highest it is actually at one of its lowest points. Some people are starting to develop a bunker mentality due to their weakened sense of security.
I spoke earlier of the sense of the general public that our judicial system is impotent. I highly respect lawyers, judges, and our judiciary. One of the main points that I hear again and again is that our laws and punishments for crimes are not only lax but seem, in the eyes of the public to be inconsistent. I am told that the parole system procedures need to be tightened. Prison sentences should be made longer and violent

June 25, 1987
Capital Punishment
criminals should be kept off the streets. Yet rehabilitation is necessary. A life sentence should be just that, a life sentence. Currently within our parole system, a 10-year sentence could actually mean six years or seven years, and even less in certain extenuating circumstances.
Furthermore; the public is often threatened by criminals once they are sentenced. I have been in a court where the criminal who was convicted has pointed a finger at the victim saying, "I will get you when I get out". These families who have been threatened are quaking in their boots in a few years, keeping their doors locked and staying inside. Repeat offenders are often released earlier than their sentence required and go back on the street to commit crimes. This is entirely unacceptable.
Our criminal justice system is in serious need of reform. The average Canadian citizen is not provided with the necessary protection to live a safe and healthy life, while criminals and murderers are allowed to remain on the streets often after serving a minimal sentence. We are often told that they are rehabilitated, but one should ask the family of a murder victim or a victim who has been badly molested, raped or grievously harmed. There are hundreds of such victims.
We as citizens and legislators must reassess what is happening in society and become sensitive to the needs and wants of our citizens. For years, many Canadians have been asking for the reinstatement of the death penalty. Legislators have not always responded to those demands.
Let us examine why the public is expressing such strong views on capital punishment. Perhaps it is the exasperation they feel with the justice system. Maybe they believe that the state should do something to protect them and give them a sense of fairness and that they have a right to live in peace and quiet.
Many representations on all sides of the issue have been made to each Member. For example, I have an open letter from a father of a first degree murder victim. Fie is Mr. Donald Sullivan of Ajax, Ontario. He wrote concerning the brutal and senseless murder of his daughter Pamela on October 22, 1980.
Pam was sexually assaulted and murdered on her way home from work one evening, right in front of her family home. She was murdered by a complete stranger who had been released by the Collins Bay Penitentiary just a week earlier, on mandatory supervision release. The theory is correct; the practice is not. This man was found guilty of first degree murder in 1981 and sentenced to imprisonment in Kingston Penitentiary. It is ironic that he became a homicide victim himself when he was killed in prison in July, 1986. He was another murder victim, but this time within the walls of our prisons. We often hear other Members say that we may be executing an innocent person, but no one seems to pay
attention to the fact that this woman was an innocent victim. She is a statistic, he had been made an anti-hero.
Mr. Sullivan writes:
I am asking you to try and wade through the rhetoric, the confusing jumble of statistics, all the graphs, numbers and try to remember that each number, each statistic, represents one who was a loved family member, a son, daughter, a wife, a mom, a husband, a dad. Numbers do not bleed; rates per thousand do not die; justice centre statistics do not have to be buried.
Mr. Sullivan, and his family, is as much a victim as his murdered daughter, Pamela.
In Edmonton we have the organization "Victims of Violence" which was founded by Gary and Sharon Rosenfeldt. The Rosenfeldts became victims of violence when their son was one of the children brutally murdered by Clifford Olson. Mr. Rosenfeldt has been to my office several times in the last two years asking for help and for us to do something to prevent crimes like this, preventing the potential of someone like Mr. Olson being released again. There are many others like Clifford Olson.
The Rosenfeldts have been lobbying legislators to become more aware and more sensitive to the plight of victims of violence. I cannot help but feel that it is wrong for Canadians to believe they must lobby for the basic right to feel secure. I am not calling for revenge or retribution, but just the right to feel safe. We as legislators must keep this in mind at all times and work to ensure that the state has the strength and the power to protect its citizens. Otherwise, we as a nation fail in our duty to protect Canadians.
Capital punishment should be an option made available in the sentencing process. There is nothing wrong with it being an option. It is the ultimate and often times the greatest and only protection that potential victims may have.
It is believed that there is a deterrence factor in having the death penalty. We have heard debate about this issue, but the Royal Commission on Capital Punishment in Great Britain heard evidence concerning criminal cases which indicated in some instances that the threat of the death penalty had acted as a deterrent to murder. In 1976, the Supreme Court of the United States considered capital punishment a significant deterrent in a number of cases.
Law enforcement authorities have contended that abolition of the death penalty increases the risk for police and prison staff. It would be reasonable to assume that in seeking to avoid arrest, a criminal would be less likely to shoot a police officer if there were a death penalty.
Growing numbers of inmates serving life sentences for first degree murder seem to increase prison violence and murder. They have nothing to lose and perhaps something small to gain. Murder rates within the penitentiary population almost doubled between 1976 and 1981, with most occurrences taking place in maximum security institutions. That is a plain fact for all to see. In 1983, participation in major security incidents was higher among first degree murderers than among the rest
June 25, 1987

of the penitentiary population. Again, it is because they have nothing to lose.
Who is in the greatest danger? First, it is prison inmates. I referred earlier to the inmate who was killed, as have many others. Prison guards and police officers are also in danger. First degree murderers have nothing to lose and can go on to participate again, raise a bit of hell to see what they can do. The logical conclusion is capital punishment.
Deterrence does not show up in statistics. By preventing a killing, the potential victim is alive and well. We never consider that this is a person who might have been killed under certain circumstances by a convicted murderer who was released. However, since we know nothing about it, it cannot be a statistic. That is something we should all consider.
Very few convicted killers will kill again after being allowed to go free. Most of them do not. Most of them are rehabilitated. But we must protect every citizen to the best of our ability. An innocent Canadian, neighbour, member of family, once killed is gone forever. It is very important that we as a country have the ability to protect our citizens.
More than 20 such innocent Canadian victims have lost their lives. I would like to read to the House a letter to the editor which appeared in yesterday's Ottawa Citizen. It is entitled "Vile Murder", and states:
I believe in capital punishment. I always have and always will. Our Sheryl, age 20, was a successful fashion model in Toronto. She was violently murdered, her face destroyed by a hammer. Ralph Powers, a stranger to Sheryl, was on mandatory supervision, having served seven of 10 years of his sentence. Powers had stalked 15 beautiful young women before he saw Sheryl. He posed as a Bell Telephone repairman to gain entry to her apartment.
Powers gave my daughter a life sentence with no chance of parole. Perhaps Powers will be released in 15 or 25 years. Is that really a life sentence for first-degree murder? I believe that Powers will kill again, as he confessed after his second attack (she escaped) that he had chosen his third and fourth victims in August 1981.
I would not want another family to go through what our family has. The pain of the violent murder of my daughter will never leave me. It is a life sentence for me and for my family and friends-with no chance of parole.
It is signed "Sally Gardner, Ottawa".
The death penalty must be returned. I thank the House for the privilege of speaking on this most important debate and look forward to a favourable response to the reinstatement of capital punishment.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REINSTATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a comment in support of my colleague's position and his concern about the justice system as it pertains to persons in prison and on parole. I would like to read into the record the most recent information from StatsCan, the Solicitor General's office, and from the Correctional Institutional report.
Since the abolition of capital punishment in 1976, there has been a 400 per cent increase in murders within our prisons. Prior to 1976, on average, there were two victims of murder in our prisons per year, that is, from 1962 through until 1976.
Capital Punishment
When we officially abolished capital punishment in 1976, the rate jumped to 28 murders in 1977, eight murders in 1978, 10 murders in 1979 and as high as 15 murders in 1984. When we average it out we find there were 100 persons murdered in our prison societies of less than 1000 in population, making an average of 11 murders per year.
That is not to mention the recent report in support of my colleague, dealing with persons on parole. The Solicitor General of the former Liberal Government has stated, "There have been a total of seven cases of repeat murderers committing the second offence while on parole".
If that is not bad enough, since that statement the Parole Board has advised me that since February of 1987, the cut-off date for the last report, there have been two more murders in Canada by murderers on parole. One of those murderers has been convicted very recently and the other has been charged with murder. His conviction is pending.
Therefore, I think not only has the parole system been an abysmal failure but it needs, as reiterated by the Chairman of our current Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General, a pretty close look at. For that reason the committee initiated a study into the parole system for the need of change. While doing so, I suggest that the justice committee take a pretty good look at our plea bargaining system within the justice system.
A lot of these people who are charged with first degree murder, plead a lesser offence of second-degree murder, receive a quick conviction and are out in 10 years after serving two-thirds of their 15-year sentence rather than going the route on the first degree charge as laid by the authorities on the basis of their investigation.
I think this liberal attitude of the justice system, the plea bargaining system, the parole system and all of these various factors, need to be closely looked at. That is not to say that by addressing those systems only we will deal effectively with the psychopathic repeat murderer who shows no remorse or regret and would willingly do it again without hesitation.
What we are looking for is capital punishment, as is my colleague, for only certain acts, the most heinous acts of planned, deliberate, premeditated murder. That is what the Canadian people want. That is what this House of Commons must respond to.
As Members of Parliament, in the interests of the protection of society, we must listen to our constituents on what they consider to be a reasonable form of justice befitting the most heinous crimes. We are not looking to execute 400 or 500 persons a year, but only those who commit murders of the most heinous nature. Robert Shantz of Vancouver who defended Clifford Olson said, "There is only one answer for Clifford Olson and that is execution". That was said by the criminal lawyer who defended Clifford Olson.
A prematurely retired criminal lawyer in British Columbia by name of Les Bewley resigned because he said one of the

June 25, 1987
Capital Punishment
most contributing factors to his displeasure with the judicial system today is the plea bargaining system between Crown prosecutors and defending lawyers. They gleefully sit behind closed doors and bargain down the most serious offences in order for a quick conviction and early release. Adjusting that system is long overdue. Mr. Les Bewley, a former criminal court judge, handed in his resignation to the Attorney General because, he said, "Plea bargaining is the venereal disease of our justice system here in Canada today".

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REINSTATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to pose a question to the Hon. Member with whose position I also agree. I also want to share some information with him. The Hon. Member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) was talking about our justice system. I would like to point out to the House that 1 had an opportunity, which perhaps other Members of the House have not, that is, the honour of serving on a jury in a trial on a murder case. There are always those people who will worry about convicting an innocent person. I would like to tell the Hon. Member that when one is serving on a jury in a trial for murder, one wants to be 150 per cent sure. If the Hon. Member sat on a jury in similar circumstances I think he would agree that if there was any doubt in his mind, he would find that person innocent. Many people will use as that reason for doubt that chance of convicting an innocent person. Having been on a jury, I can tell the House that it is the most excruciating experience one could possibly go through, and if there is any doubt in one's mind, the person certainly would not be convicted.
I am sure the Hon. Member's constituents will say to him that they are opposed to capital punishment in general, but in specific cases, yes, they would agree to capital punishment. How does the Hon. Member answer that? Can we have a partial bringing back of capital punishment only for those specific cases? How do we bring it back on the books so it would apply to those heinous crimes talked about by the Hon. Member himself and the Hon. Member for Peterborough? We are in a bit of a dilemma in that situation in which many people oppose the death penalty. However, there are those who are in favour, in particular cases. How would the Hon. Member answer constituents concerns in this particular area?

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REINSTATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am certainly pleased to respond to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Essex-Kent (Mr. Caldwell). This is indeed a dilemma. I appreciate that the Hon. Member has asked me about it. I appreciate the dilemma of our constituents, the people outside this House. Nothing is perfect. We cannot guarantee anything. For that matter, we might walk out of the House and be run over by a vehicle and become an accident victim. So life is gone.
However, my contention is, and I believe it is the contention of most citizens with whom I have spoken, that the state should have the prerogative, in the wisdom of the judge and jury, to mete out the ultimate penalty. If that terrible crime is committed then the state must have capital punishment on its
books. The person will receive the death penalty and that will be the end of the case.
There is nothing wrong with the state having this prerogative, or to carry it out for the protection of its citizens. As my colleague from Peterborough has mentioned, there are many areas which we should consider, including the judiciary, the parole system, and capital punishment in the over-all context of what is the best and most fair for our citizens.
Of course, citizens will always ask, "What about this particular case", or "What about that particular case?" It is up to the judiciary in its wisdom, with or without a jury, to make a decision. A decision is made and we will have to live with it. We must be strong and firm. We must also be compassionate.
This is why I believe that the state has to have this prerogative, so that we can proceed with it rather than appear as impotent legislators, or impotent judges or impotent police. This is why the people are out there screaming, "Do something". This is one step, and it is a positive one. It is what I believe to be the right step.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REINSTATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope that I shall be able to continue my speech and use the rest of my 20 minutes after the Oral Question Period.
It is with a great deal of interest that I take part in the debate on capital punishment. I would like to touch on several points. First, I wish to speak about the reasons for which this Government decided to hold this debate. Second, if I may, I would like to review some of the speeches we have heard in this House on the death penalty, and finally, to express my own views on reinstatement of the death penalty.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I must tell you that the Member for Temiscamingue is against the death penalty, and I know that most of my colleagues already know where I stand on this issue.
We have been strongly criticized by the opposition Parties for holding a debate on the death penalty during this Parliament. However, it should be pointed out that the Progressive Conservative Party had made a commitment to hold such a debate during the 1984 campaign. In passing, Mr. Speaker, while I am speaking about the commitments made by the Progressive Conservative Party during the 1984 election campaign, I would like to say that we have a quite enviable record as far as respecting those commitments is concerned. On which themes did the Progressive Conservative Party base its campaign during the summer of 1984? There were three major themes in our campaign. The first was national reconciliation, and with the constitutional agreement signed recently by the 11 first ministers of Canada, I believe that we can say that national reconciliation is now a fact. Another major theme of our campaign was reduction of our enormous national deficit, which severely restricts the freedom of movement of the federal Government. In this regard, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Government have done a remarkable job. A third major theme of our campaign was economic recovery, and I believe that, objectively, everyone will have to admit that our economy is now definitely in better shape, with nearly 800,000 jobs created, a very active economic sector and prosperous businesses. I have the feeling that, within a few months, we shall be able to say that one million jobs have been created.
What was said about the death penalty issue during the 1984 electoral campaign? The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) had promised that there would be a free debate in the House during our mandate. Saying that such a debate was unwarranted would be completely inaccurate since the death penalty issue has aroused the interest of Canadians for decades and has already been discussed in this House. Parliament has had to examine the death penalty issue on many occasions, as have many other Parliaments, for instance in Great Britain, where this issue has also been discussed many times, including few months ago when Parliament voted against reinstatement of the death penalty in Great Britain.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the Government was justified in reopening this debate as many Canadians wanted to discuss the issue of the death penalty and as such a debate can bring new light on this issue. Whatever the solution chosen by this Government, it will have been worthwhile having an open and enlightened debate in this House. Naturally, I must say that I sincerely hope that this Government and this Parliament will vote against reinstatement of the death penalty in Canada. If they do, Mr. Speaker, the debate will still have been useful as it will have been carried out in an enlightened manner and the Canadian public will perhaps be better informed about the issues involved.
In my opinion, it is extremely important in such a debate to respect the opinion of others. The debate should remain objective, and it is essential to respect the views of others even though they might not be our own. Mr. Speaker, how is Canadian public opinion represented in the House in the debate on the death penalty?
From the views I have heard expressed in this House, I believe that the Progressive Conservative Party is truly representative of public opinion on the death penalty. You would have to be blind to say that public opinion is not very divided on whether to reinstate the death penalty or not, and it is our own party which best represents this plurality of opinions.
As you are about to interrupt me, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that I shall perhaps be back after the Oral Question Period to conclude my speech and explain to the House the basic reasons why I am personally vigourously opposed to reinstatement of the death penalty.

subsubtopic: NICARAGUA-CONTRA ATTACK ON CANADIAN-AID PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have previously asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to condemn the American-backed Contras as terrorists. Their destruction of a Canadian-aid project in the small village of Macotol, Nicaragua, was a crime ending in the slaughter of innocent men, women and children. The Secretary of State for External Affairs assured me that he would raise the matter with U.S. Secretary of State

June 25, 1987
George Shultz when he met with him, in either Venice or Reykajavik.
The Minister's response is of great concern to Canadian non-governmental organizations in light of the fact that the U.S.-backed rebels, on June 19, attacked a state supervised farming community in Los Millones, Nicaragua, killing eight and robbing the community of food and medical supplies.
Indeed, this was not a Canadian-aid project but the Contras' track record of attacking innocent villagers is bound to happen again and again.
Canadians are aware that they are working in a hostile environment in Nicaragua, but they do not need the extra burden that comes with our American neighbours backing rebels to attack, kill and destroy the lives and property of noncombatant people who already face a daily struggle to survive.
I am calling upon the Secretary of State for External Affairs to inform the House publicly and the Canadian people of his meeting with Secretary of State George Shultz regarding the action, if any, the U.S. proposes to undertake to prevent this slaughter of innocent peasants.
Also, will the Minister tell the House whether he informed the Reagan administration that Canada will pursue its own course of action through the United Nations if the U.S. does not improve the situation?

subtopic: ACID RAIN-COMMITTEE MEMBERS' VISIT TO UNITED STATES CONGRESS
ACID RAIN-COMMITTEE MEMBERS' VISIT TO UNITED STATES CONGRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Special Committee on Acid Rain returned home from Washington last night after discussions with members of the U.S. Congress and environmental officials.
Time and again committee members were assured that Canada's persistence toward achieving acid rain controls is playing a crucial role in the United States.
Senator George Mitchell of Maine, who has an acid rain control Bill before Congress, said that our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is directly responsible for changing President Reagan's attitude on this important issue.
The Senator pointed out, as did other Congressmen, that the only times the President has spoken in favour of acid rain abatement were in the presence of the Prime Minister.
For this reason, acid rain control proponents in the U.S. are urging Canada to keep the pressure on.
Our fears were confirmed in meetings with the State Department, the Environmental Protection Agency, and the National Coal Association, whose representatives are less than enthusiastic about controls.
On the other hand, Canadians can rest assured that the efforts put forth by the Prime Minister are echoing through the halls of Capitol Hill.
The appearance of the special committee, showing political solidarity among all federal Parties, is yet another indication that Canada expects real action in the form of U.S. acid rain controls.

subtopic: REQUEST GOVERNMENT PROVIDE FUNDS TO SATISFY ORGANIZATIONS' REQUIREMENTS
REQUEST GOVERNMENT PROVIDE FUNDS TO SATISFY ORGANIZATIONS' REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise concerning job planning projects for seriously underprivileged people in respect to employment.
Many agencies are rightly wondering why the Department of Employment and Immigration continues publicizing such a program when in fact, as confirmed by the Minister's office, no monies are now available to support new initiatives for job integration of seriously underprivileged persons.
What right has the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) to so mislead the people and agencies involved by making available to them literature pubicizing on programs they will never be able to access because the funds needed are not there, unless an already committed agency withdraws?
We are faced with an unacceptable situation, Mr. Speaker, and I am asking the Minister to correct that gap as soon as possible and inject extra money to meet the needs of agencies that had applications turned down for that reason, after having their appetite whetted by enticing literature.

subtopic: OPPOSITION TO EMPLOYEE REDUCTIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
OPPOSITION TO EMPLOYEE REDUCTIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, two weeks ago I made a statement in the House regarding the reduction of 102 employee positions in Saskatoon and Melville by the Canadian National Railways.
In response to my statement a meeting was held last week, in Saskatoon, with a Vice-President of CN. However, we unfortunately could not reach a decision that satisfied all parties involved in the discussions.
I clearly understand CN's need to down-size its operations and encourage early retirement to make its rail service more
June 25, 1987

cost efficient, but I must let the facts speak for themselves. Over 14 per cent of CN's revenues come from Saskatchewan. That contribution is more than the combined revenues of all of the maritime provinces, the Northwest Territories, and the Province of Manitoba.
Wheat will continue to be a major export out of the province, and an increase in the production of potash and coal, as shown in economic forecasts, promises a wider use of CN facilities in the future.
It may carry out the down-sizing of its labour force. However, I insist that CN not transfer those employees to Winnipeg and close up repair shops that will be increasingly important to CN and Saskatchewan's future.

subtopic: ALCAN CORPORATION-REDUCTION OF WATER FLOW INTO SALMON-RICH B.C. RIVERS
ALCAN CORPORATION-REDUCTION OF WATER FLOW INTO SALMON-RICH B.C. RIVERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1980 residents in northwest British Columbia were shocked to hear that Alcan allowed little more than a trickle of water to be released over its Skins Lake Spillway into the salmon-rich Nechako and Fraser rivers.
Under public pressure from farmers, communities, recrea-tionalists, Indian bands, and commercial and sports fishermen, a Supreme Court injunction forced Alcan to provide minimal water flows.
The injunction was renewed annually until 1985, when Alcan sought exclusive jurisdiction over a publicly-owned river. With private profits to be made from the export of raw power, Alcan wants to hoard the water for its own hidden agenda.
The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) has now sold out to Alcan with a private deal on water flows at only one-half of what his own scientists filed in court as the minimum required.
One cannot adequately convey the level of betrayal ordinary British Columbians feel upon hearing that the Minister of Fisheries has sold out the public trust.
The salmon industry is worth over $500 million a year. The Minister has failed to exercise the responsibility granted to him under Section 29(10) of the Fisheries Act and to ensure that proper water flows are maintained. The Minister must immediately hold public hearings into the required flow regime and ensure that no green light be given to Kemano 2 without a public approval process.
No such initiative has been forthcoming from the Minister who must now resign. He is allowing our salmon resource to be ruined.
It is totally unacceptable and irresponsible for the Minister to stand in the House under the charade of representing the fisheries ministry while he ignores his legal mandate, neglects his responsibilities to the fisheries resource, and guts the Canadian public trust.

subtopic: IMPORTANCE OF RAILWAY NETWORK IN ABITIBI
IMPORTANCE OF RAILWAY NETWORK IN ABITIBI
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after considering the CN's application to abandon the line in the Chapais-Franquet subdivision in Abitibi, the CTC's Committee, further to a decision dated January 22, 1979, concluded:
"Railways may file grant applications in respect of branch lines, provided that a line not covered by an application would not in effect be isolated from the remaining system, were the line covered by the application to be abandoned".
That Chapais subdivision would be rerouted to a longer haul through via the CN's Cran subdivision in Lac Saint-Jean. It appears this would be a case of unacceptable line division as specified by the CTC. The CN was to file with the CTC on June 22, 1987, further argument concerning their application.
The long distances between Canadian regions are for us Abitibians an enormous challenge to knowing and understanding one another, and we cannot legislate geography. The railway system has helped Abitibi overcome that difficulty.
Mr. Speaker, this is a first victory for the CN's workers, people in Senneterre, all economic partners in the Abitibi- Temiscamingue economy and for myself. We are proud to be Abitibians.

maintopic: DAY TRIPPERS' PURCHASES OF MILK FROM UNITED STATES- EFFECT ON DAIRY INDUSTRY
DAY TRIPPERS' PURCHASES OF MILK FROM UNITED STATES- EFFECT ON DAIRY INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, "Welcome to the Land of Milk and Honey and Cheap Gas", that is the 20-foot billboard which greets British Columbians as they near the Douglas border crossing into the United States.
The price of American milk is attractive to budget-minded shoppers, but B.C. dairymen cannot compete with the current

June 25, 1987
heavy subsidies within the U.S. industry. Canadians pay 90 per cent of the true cost of milk at the dairy case, while American shoppers only contribute two-thirds.
Using the Customs count of 12,000 border crossings every day, the B.C. dairy industry estimates that it loses about $70 million every year in lost sales. The New Brunswick dairy industry has similar problems because of its geography.
Dairy producers in British Columbia and New Brunswick want Customs and Excise to enforce the 17.5 per cent duty on goods purchased in the United States when travellers have been out of the country for less than 24 hours, in order to keep our farm producers on an equal footing with American dairy farmers.

Mr. Speaker, Canada's lead in space will be maintained. The Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) is in Toronto today announcing a 10-year support program for the Canadian Radarsat.
Based on the immense and diverse geography in Canada, our scientists have continuously developed remote sensing technologies to the point where Radarsat is recognized as the leading edge in this field for the monitoring of ice floes, the assessment of environmental developments, the forecasting of our weather, and the evaluation of our natural resources.
This is a collective and collaborative achievement on the part of many federal government Departments, the provinces, the United Kingdom, and the United States.
Let us salute the Minister and the Government as Canada continues its lead in space with Radarsat.

Mr. Speaker, today, as the House of Commons is making itself acquainted with a new legislation on official languages, it is important to remember that June 25, 1987 marks another important anniversary in the history of Franco-Ontarians.
Regulation 17, announced to the Ontario legislature on April 13, 1912, we implemented on June 25 of that same year. Unfortunately, that regulation prohibited for all practical purposes French education in Ontario.
Many Franco-Ontarians no doubt remember the period that followed the implementation of that legislation. Indeed, more
than 200,000 French-speaking citizens of Ontario were deprived during almost 15 years of French instruction.
1 am sure that all Members of this House will want to join me in paying tribute to all those who fought against the implementation of that rule and especially one of my predecessors, the late Aurelien Belanger, provincial Member for the riding of Prescott.
I would like to mention the historian, Mr. Paul-Franqois Sylvestre who underlined recently the 75th anniversary of that infamous regulation 17.

Northern Development signed an order finally recognizing as Indian bands six communities of the Nisnawbe-Aski nation; namely, Aroland, Kee-Way-Win, Wawakapewin, New Slate Falls, McDowell Lake and Saugeen.
