subtopic: ACID RAIN-BENEFICIAL EFFECT OF NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD'S RULING ON ELECTRICITY EXPORTS
ACID RAIN-BENEFICIAL EFFECT OF NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD'S RULING ON ELECTRICITY EXPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the decision of the National Energy Board to reject Hydro Quebec's application to sell electricity was well timed for the acid rain committee's visit to Washington, D.C. this week. Some American legislators have charged in the past that Canada wants tough acid rain controls in the United States to shut down U.S. dirty coal plants and open up a larger market for Canadian electricity exports. The ruling of the National Energy Board has helped to put that ludicrous conspiracy theory to rest.
The NEB ruling has implications in Canada too. Increased sales of Hydro Quebec power to Canadian provinces would reduce reliance on coal-fired power plants in Ontario and in the Maritimes thus helping to reduce acid rain pollution. Larger sales of hydro electricity in Canada would reduce pressure for more nuclear power plants now being considered in New Brunswick and Ontario.
Quebec's Energy Minister is to be congratulated for announcing that Quebec hydro-power will be offered to Canadian provinces first. He would best protect the environment and the national interest if Quebec Hydro offers electricity to the provinces at the same price as it offers it to American clients.

June 25, 1987
Oral Questions

subtopic: OPPORTUNITY TO INVITE AMERICANS TO PRESSURE THEIR REPRESENTATIVES

Mr. Speaker, the Special Committee on Acid Rain has just returned from Washington, where, during two days of intensive sessions, the Committee met with major U.S., environmental groups and with senators and members of the House of Representatives who are involved in the fight against acid rain.
The message brought by our delegation was very clear: Stop polluting us, act on your promises and reduce pollution-causing emissions.
Mr. Speaker, everyone the Committee met insisted that the pressure put by the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) on the President of the United States was to have encouraging results. In fact, a number of Bills are now on the table, and if any of these were to be passed, it would be a great victory for Canada.
However, much remains to be done, and the Americans gave us a very clear message that our Government and Canadians should continue to put strong pressure on the U.S. Administration.
Mr. Speaker, why do we not take advantage of the summer holidays to urge all the Americans we meet to put pressure on their elected representatives? That is the only way we are going to win.

Mr. Speaker, we are not often called upon to debate a fundamental question of life and death. The question of the restoration of capital punishment is exactly that question. This House will be deciding whether there are circumstances in which the state is justified, in the criminal justice system, in taking a human life.
I want to disagree strongly with the Hon. Member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Desjardins) who has just indicated that he believes 50 hours of debate is enough and that all Members who would want to speak should have done so within 50 hours. We on our side know that that is not the case. We have a very long list. Ministers have made three attempts now to prevent all Members who want to speak from doing so. We seem to be in a hiatus now between their plots of one kind and another to bring this debate to a close.
If the Hon. Member favours abolition, I urge him to support the continuation of this debate as long as possible because the effect of it seems to be to encourage a number of Members who thought otherwise to have second thoughts and begin to see that capital punishment is not the solution which many believe it is.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, you may find it ironic that the Member for York Centre, that is myself, am what I like to call an abolitionist, but an abolitionist with one exception in which I feel that capital punishment is justified. I hope in my remarks today to be able to indicate the circumstances in which I support capital punishment. They are exactly the same circumstances in which I supported it in 1976. In the intervening time I had the opportunity to be the Solicitor General of Canada responsible for Canada's penitentiaries. That which I learned in that job, about which I want to speak soon, has confirmed my feelings that capital punishment, in one narrow area of the law, would actually save lives. I believe that with due respect to human life the use of capital punishment is not justified except where it can be shown that it will actually save lives.

June 25, 1987
Capital Punishment
Before I turn to my own views on capital punishment, I want to make some comments about this debate in general. I do not favour this debate. I am voting against the resolution because I believe the debate has been used to distract attention from very important areas of public policy, not only the performance of the Government but even ways of improving our criminal justice system.
1 think the effect that capital punishment will have in the criminal justice system is small compared to all the other things we can do to make our criminal justice system better. I condemn the Government for focusing on this one issue, particularly under the administration of a Prime Minister who is an admitted abolitionist and is taking a position before the country which may well see capital punishment restored.
I will deal with my concern about the debate of the issue by dealing with the two sides of the issue. First, among those who support capital punishment-and I refer to many millions of Canadians-I find that in their position is a sense of desperation, that while they are not confident that capital punishment will work in reducing the murder rate, it will have a beneficial effect on law and order in society. I sympathize very much with that view, but I think it is wrong.
I do not believe that restoring capital punishment will do very much outside the area of murder, yet I have heard Members say in the House that having capital punishment is the corner-stone of an effective criminal justice system. It is as if to say there would be less other crimes if capital punishment were on the books, and there would be more law and order in society. Because people have that view about capital punishment, I think it gets the support of people who, when they look at it as a remedy, fundamentally do not really believe that it will do a significant job in the criminal justice system.
I have heard others say that the reason they support capital punishment is a fear that people who are sentenced to life imprisonment for murder will get out on parole and be back on the streets in a few years, ready to murder again. I want to tell those people something that I do not think they will believe but is absolutely true. We have on the statute books of Canada today a penalty for murder which is as effective as capital punishment. It is the life sentence.
I know that people say they have read about criminals who get out, but I want to state categorically to those who support capital punishment on this ground that no one in Canada who has ever been sentenced to the stiffest penalty that was added to our law in 1976 has been released from penitentiary. All of them, except those who have died since 1976, are still in prison. We read about people who committed murders getting out of jail, but if one checks into it, one will see that these are people who are not sentenced to the maximum penalty.
The Member for Temiscamingue was wrong about that as well. He said that the 25-year sentence means that people may
apply for parole after seven years, and argued that it should be increased to 16 or 17 years. That is not a 25-year sentence. It is a full life sentence, except that after 25 years one has the right to go before a judge and ask for permission to apply for parole. It does not mean that parole will be granted by the judge or a parole board. None of those people will even be eligible to apply until the year 2001. None of them have done so. The idea that people who get the maximum sentence known to the law now are getting out and committing other murders is absolutely wrong.
I say to those who support capital punishment on that ground that they should look again. There is a very good, equal deterrent in the law in the form of the full life sentence that was introduced by my colleague, the Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), when he was Solicitor General in 1976.
I want to say something to the abolitionists because I find something peculiar in their position as well. Abolitionist after abolitionist will stand up and say that while they are an abolitionist, they believe our criminal justice system is lousy and needs to be fundamentally changed. They seem to want to defend their support for abolition in the face of the retentionist by agreeing somehow or other that we have a lousy system of criminal justice that is not working. I think they are also wrong.
1 speak as one who knows something about the criminal justice system. I am not saying that it cannot be improved, but it is not correct to say that it is fundamentally wrong, that sentences are too low and making changes to the criminal justice system will produce much less crime in society.
I have ideas for improving the criminal justice system. I introduced some, in the area of crime prevention for example, while 1 was Solicitor General. I believe crime can be reduced much more easily by preventing it from happening than by the way we handle criminals, whether it is putting them in prison or diverting them. I tried to encourage the movement of the criminal justice system into crime prevention. There is not much room to make our criminal justice system do a very much better job for us. While we read about those things that go wrong, let me suggest that they are as much a function of the human condition as they are of the criminal justice system. Unlike some other countries, such as the United States, we have control of our criminal justice system.
I suggest to those abolitionists who are telling people that there is a magic solution to making the criminal justice system prevent all crime that they are wrong and misleading people in trying to convince them that capital punishment is not the answer and that there is some magic key when the fact is that crime is related to the human condition. We are making our best efforts to try to fight crime.
If there was a key to tremendous reductions and great improvements in running our prisons, dealing with criminals or altering sentences, I think we would have found it years ago.
June 25, 1987

There is a very strong will in Canadian society to improve the criminal justice system.
While I do not mean to sound like a Conservative by saying we have to defend what exists, I believe steps can be taken to improve it but not enough to deliver on the commitments of some abolitionists who are saying that we must scrap this system and start again. It is a good system that serves the Canadian people rather well, even though I think it can be improved a lot.
One of the reasons I condemn the Government for bringing this resolution forward is that I feel so strongly that we should be looking at the criminal justice system. We should be studying the report of the Sentencing Commission. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) says that he is against capital punishment, but instead of dealing with the report of the Sentencing Commission, which makes some sensible recommendations for improving the system, he is giving the House a capital punishment debate that is detached from any inspection of alternatives to capital punishment which might help people make up their minds as to whether or not they are in favour of capital punishment.
I have indicated that I am voting against the resolution and have given my reasons. Now I want to explain the reason I support capital punishment in the area in which I believe it will be effective.
I stated my belief that a full life sentence as already established in our law is as effective as capital punishment. However, there is a growing number of murders committed by people who are not deterred by a full life sentence. The reason they are not deterred is that they are already serving a full life sentence. These are people who have been sentenced since 1976 to spending their natural life in prison. The statistics which were released in a summary form a few weeks ago by the Ministry of Solicitor General show that the murder rate in our penitentiaries is astronomical. It is the duty of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) to protect inmates from being killed by other inmates during their sentence, and to protect guards and officials from being killed by inmates during the time they are in prison. That protection is not being afforded now.
While I may be criticized for saying this, the officials do not even try to solve most of the murders that take place in prisons because everyone knows who is responsible for a murder when it is committed. The prison is too small that the knowledge of the identity of the killer is not known. Yet, the philosophy must be: "Why bother trying to solve this murder?"
Why bother singling out an inmate, charging him again, having an expensive police investigation, a trial, putting the inmate up in a hotel, eating in restaurants, getting his picture in the papers, and all this, including his lawyer, paid for by the taxpayers, and then at the end, after the conviction-and I could actually name a few inmates who have gone through this process-back he goes to prison to continue the sentence he
Capital Punishment
was serving before he committed the murder. I think we have a responsibility within the criminal justice system to deal with that problem.
I know there are those who feel they are not convinced that capital punishment is a deterrent but who say that if they could be convinced, they would support it. I want to urge those people to reflect on this situation and on the problem of dealing with the offender already sentenced to serving life.
We hear people say from time to time that capital punishment in their view is not a deterrent. I think that is a very foolish thing to say. Certainly, it is true to a point. Capital punishment is not a deterrent to the 99.9 per cent of Canadians who would never think of killing anyone, even if it was not a crime. Those people are not deterred by the idea of capital punishment. They are deterred by the respect they have for life and by the feeling of horror they have against killing anyone.
Among those people who have a potential under some circumstances to commit a murder, I think capital punishment is a deterrent. The knowledge they have that they could be caught and, if caught, their life would be taken, must surely figure into their calculations. Common sense tells us it does. Therefore, it is a deterrent.
The point I make, though, is that I do not see how one could consider it to be a more effective deterrent than life imprisonment. I think they are equal, especially when "life" is, as I said, full life. Capital punishment is a deterrent, one which involves taking a human life, but comparing it to the equally effective deterrent which does not involve taking a human life, I think one has to choose the latter. That is why I support full life imprisonment for the kinds of murders which are defined in the Criminal Code, with one exception.
I want to close by suggesting to you, Mr. Speaker, that I think I can characterize myself as an abolitionist, as one who would oppose capital punishment except that I am convinced, from my knowledge of prisons and from my experience with the violent murders which take place there on an increasing basis, that capital punishment is justified in those circumstances.
I want to say another word on a subject which perhaps many have not thought about. I think if we introduce capital punishment, it would be unacceptable to the Canadian people if it resulted in a great number of executions. If there are 700 murders a year and if there were 500 or so people convicted of murder, anyone who wants to suggest there should be 500 executions a year in Canada would be putting an appalling proposition forward. I wonder if the Hon. Member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) has ever taken a pencil to his theory to see how many executions there would be if capital punishment was reinstated? I think there would be something abhorrent to me of several executions taking place a year. I would find that appalling in a civilized country such as ours.
On the other hand, if the Members who favour capital punishment were content to see it applied only in the area

June 25, 1987
Capital Punishment
where I have suggested it is logical, because there is no other alternative, then the number of executions which would occur would be very small. I think if there were one in five years, or seven years, it would be as much as one could possibly expect. I think that is a factor. 1 know that those who favour capital punishment, if the statistics are right as this debate has proceeded, are having some second thoughts about it.
I think one of the calculations must surely be what is happening in the United States where recent hurdles have been cleared with respect to cases before the Supreme Court and where 1,400 convicted murderers may be executed in the next several months. The prospect of that appalling number of executions taking place in a democratic country is in itself a great deterrent to the restoration of capital punishment. If this resolution carries, I would urge all of those who are going to sit on the committee to bear in mind that Canadians, even those who have supported capital punishment, would be tremendously disturbed to see anymore than a very, very small number of executions take place.
With those thoughts, I am pleased to be able to participate in the debate and look forward to the Government changing its mind about its agenda. If this resolution is not to be withdrawn, and frankly I would prefer to see it withdrawn, I hope all of those who wish to speak to it would be given the opportunity to do so.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may, I would like to put a question to the Hon Member. Much of what he has said in the House today one can find in similar terms in the speech he gave to this House on May 19, 1976, the last time there was such a debate on the question of capital punishment. My question will be along two lines. I find there is a bit of a contrast in what the Hon. Member has said this afternoon. In 1976 the Hon. Member said:
I suggest that public opinion is an extremely important factor in the determination of an issue like capital punishment.
He went on to say:
I do not see how any Member of this House can escape the undeniable fact that the majority of the people of Canada are of the opinion-however you want to measure or count it-that there is a place for capital punishment in our system of justice. I insist that this House must respond to that concern.
The Hon. Member has just said he would prefer to see this resolution withdrawn. Is he today feeling differently from the way he felt on May 19, 1976 when he stated: "I insist that this House must respond to the public concern that there should be capital punishment in our system"?

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REINSTATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know if the Hon. Member listened to the whole of my speech, but at the beginning I made some points about what I thought might be done to improve our war against crime in Canadian society. I suggested that capital punishment was not a large part of the solution, it was a very small part, and that time would be better spent on other things. I visualized a capital punishment debate being a very lengthy one. That is the reason I would
prefer to see the resolution withdrawn than continue in order that we could deal with crime in other ways.
I also think that public opinion is volatile and I invite the Hon. Member to notice that just in the last few months public opinion in support of capital punishment is beginning to decline. As I suggested, I think it will continue to decline as a great number of executions begin to take place in the United States and Canadians get to see who gets executed when a society introduces capital punishment and when it is applied on a very large scale.
Fundamentally, I agree with what I said in 1976. I am glad to have it read. I have not looked at it myself for awhile. What I would have to say is that in a final analysis in a democracy, the population is entitled to the kind of criminal justice system they want.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REINSTATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member on this subject. I preface my question by saying that I have taken part in a debate on capital punishment in this House on two previous occasions. I expressed my reservations about what we were doing on both those occasions. The first time in 1973 was with regard to the fact that we were entering into another five-year-trial period and I did not feel that we should have an additional trial period, that we should move to abolition right away. The second time in 1976 was with regard to the fact that in compensation for the removal of the death penalty, the Government was introducing a maximum penalty of 25 years before parole, or life.
I would like to focus on what the Hon. Member said in his comments since the reservation I expressed in 1976 was that that 25-year period as a minimum was the wrong move to take. In fact, at that time I said:
-two specific findings of criminal research-shows first, that convicted murderers have low recidivism rates, and second, the longer the imprisonment, the slimmer the chances of rehabilitation.
If the Hon. Member is saying that in the ensuing years since capital punishment was abolished he has seen a larger number of murders within the prison system, I want to ask him whether or not he figures that this lengthy penalty which was imposed at that time was wrong. Should it have been imposed and should we be moving today to re-examine the sentencing procedure so that that act which was taken at that time is reduced? Should we go back to the previous situation so that we do not escalate the difficulties within the prison system, about which I appreciate he knows, and which I know, by continuing this minimum sentence of 25 years for first-degree murder?

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REINSTATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not agree with the proposition that the minimum of 25 years should be reduced. I know it works terrible hardship for some of the people who are sentenced to it, but they have committed a very grievous offence. I think that life imprisonment is a reasonable penalty
June 25, 1987

for someone who commits a murder as defined by that section of the Act and where that penalty is invoked.
The Eton. Member wants to draw some conclusions from the fact with which I concede that the longer a person stays in prison the more likely they are to become recidivists. But what does that mean? Who gets long sentences? It is people who have committed more serious crimes. I would say that people who have committed more serious crimes are more likely to become recidivists. Murder is an exception, and I would like to say a word about that.
However, when we take the run of criminals going through the courts receiving their sentences, the longer the sentence they receive is a reflection of their character and the kind of crime they have committed. I think the resulting fact that there is a higher rate of recidivism among those people is not necessarily as a result of the time that they spend in prison but the kind of person they were and the kind of crimes they committed for which they were sentenced.
Murderers include two very different categories of person. Most of the murders that are committed in Canada are committed by people who have not committed other kinds of crimes, people who are not in the criminal culture. They are people who commit crimes of passion, although deliberately, or they would not be convicted. They are people who are responsible for what they did but who are of a sort who have not been involved in criminal activity before. Those individuals have a low rate of recidivism. They are very easy offenders to look after in prison. They are sentenced to low-level security institutions. They lead useful lives behind bars. I would not reduce the length of time they have to spend in prison because of what they did and because of the deterrent that I think ought to apply to them.
There is another category of murderer, the remorseless contract killer who is driven to it. In our maximum security prisons these are the individuals who create the problems. These are the ones who are frequently responsible for other murders. If they can be charged and properly convicted of committing a second murder in prison, then their removal from the maximum security institution will have a beneficial effect on that institution. It will reduce the jeopardy of guards, many of whom are constituents of the Hon. Member. It will remove the jeopardy of other inmates being killed. I think we owe it to them to reflect on the effect that capital punishment will have if imposed on those in prison who kill again.
Perhaps the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) has been in prisons more times than I have been in prisons, although I was in a great number of them during the time I was Solicitor General. I had a lot of time to talk to offenders, guards and officials. She will know, while perhaps most Canadians do not, that in a maximum security institution these are the toughest offenders in Canada. Most of them are trying to stay out of trouble. Some of them go through the day tense, trying to avoid getting into situations in which they will do anything but easy time with the possibility
Capital Punishment
of being paroled and getting out on good behaviour and so on. The trouble with them is that in the maximum security institutions they do not have the ability to stay out of trouble. They have been raised or directed in a way in which they respond with violence to any kind of provocation or harassment or aggression, the kind of things that a Member of Parliament, when they happen to him or her, can turn into a positive direction. Inmates in maximum security prisons cannot. They blow up. That is why, after having been convicted, they are in maximum security instead of being at lower levels. But they are provoked by this smaller group of trouble-makers in each of the maximum security institutions.
I would urge the Hon. Member, for all the respect that I have for her commitment to abolition, to recognize that where capital punishment is a deterrent, where it will have the effect of saving lives, that however distasteful she may find it, and I find it distasteful as well, I think one has to recognize that there is a place for it. If it were here, as distasteful as it is, other people would be alive who are innocent in that circumstance and who deserve the protection of the law.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when the last person was hung in Canada, and I believe there were two of them at the same time, in 1962,1 was 11 years old. In the intervening quarter of a century I feel that I have had the privilege of growing up in, becoming an adult in and becoming a Member of Parliament in one of the most nonviolent societies in the world.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REINSTATEMENT
speechtext: The murder rate has doubled!

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REINSTATEMENT
speechtext:
The murder rate has not doubled, despite what the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) says. I hope he will give me the courtesy of hearing me out. The fact remains that Canada is one of the most non-violent societies in the world. I am proud of that. I think all Members of the House should keep it in mind when we are talking about what kind of Canada we might be embarking upon if this resolution were to pass. I am of the view that the passage of this resolution would be a step toward not a less violent society but a more violent society.
I think it is ironic that as we move toward the end of this debate, whether it be tomorrow, Monday or Tuesday, or whatever the case may be, that what is shaping up is that this resolution which people once thought would carry by a significant majority may either be defeated or may pass by an insignificant margin, by a very small margin, and even then unenthusiastically.
I sense that there are Members of Parliament who feel cornered by their past statements on capital punishment and who feel cornered by various arguments as to how they ought to respond to the wishes of their constituents. Having listened

June 25, 1987
Capital Punishment
to the debate and having been a party to the public debate which has been ongoing since this resolution came before the House, they are no longer as sure of their position as they once were. Those are the Members to whom I am addressing my remarks.
I appeal to those Members to think very carefully about their responsibility as Members of Parliament.
1 know there are some who have said to themselves: "Well, I will vote for this motion now, because it is not a motion that actually reinstates capital punishment. I will vote for this motion now and, in doing so, will be consistent with what I have said before, and privately hope that the time for actually reinstating capital punishment will not come to pass; that somehow in the course of things a Bill proposing the reinstatement of capital punishment will not come before the House."
In that way, they will not actually have to vote on the reinstatement of capital punishment but will still be able to live up to some of the political commitments they have made-and some people in this House have made political commitments in that respect going back more than a decade, to the time of the last vote on capital punishment.
I ask those Members who feel that way to vote against this motion now, thus preventing what I would consider to be the possibility of a very grim road show, where a committee of this Parliament would be travelling around the country debating the relative merits of hanging people as opposed to electrocuting them, as opposed to lethal injection, or whatever other methods may be considered-something which I think would be degrading in terms of the public discourse and the general level of political and public debate in this country.
The argument for capital punishment, for the return of the death penalty, is a classic example of false expectations. There will be no decrease in violence in our society as a result of the return of the death penalty. The roots of violence and disrespect for human life are deep and complicated, and hanging a few people every year will not help. While it may make some of us feel better when a particularly vicious and obviously guilty murderer is executed, it will not stop violence in our society. It will in fact increase it, as people lose the example of a state that is not prepared to condone killing as a solution to the problem of violence in society.
The Canadian Coalition Opposed to the Death Penalty puts the question starkly and powerfully: Why kill people who kill people to show that killing people is wrong?
In 1975, the year prior to the total abolition of capital punishment in Canada, there were 701 homicides in Canada, for a rate of 3.09 per 100,000; in 1985, there were 686 homicides in Canada, for a rate of 2.78. Between those dates, Canada reported a low of 593 homicides in 1980, for a rate of 2.47.
I have read some of the speeches that have been made during the course of this debate and I am aware of the distinction that needs to be made between first degree murder
and second degree murder and the fact that there may have been a slight increase in the number of first degree murders. But, it is the second degree murders which tend to be reported in such a way that people are left with the sense that violence is on the increase, thus bringing about an increased sense of insecurity. Therefore, these figures are relevant, despite that distinction, as it is in response to the sense that there is an over-all increase in violence that many people take a position in favour of capital punishment.
The argument that the death penalty deters murder is certainly true, in the strict sense that those who are executed will certainly never murder again. I am not going to argue against that one, Mr. Speaker. Yet, this fact has to be weighed against the fact that repeat murderers constitute a very small minority of those convicted. Most murders are still committed by those who are too angry, too insane, or otherwise caught up in the moment to care whether or not they get caught and are subject to execution, or by people who do not intend to get caught, in any event.
There is also the fact that bringing back capital punishment may actually cause some murderers to go free, as judges and juries become more reluctant to convict if there is any doubt at all, or sometimes even if there is not any doubt at all, when they know that their decision will lead to the taking of a human life.
Our criminal justice system, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said the other day, is an imperfect and fallible process, like everything else run by human beings. Yet, the decision to punish an individual with death is one of an absolute nature. Not only is there the possibility of punishing the wrong person in this absolute and irretrievable way, but there is also the fact that the death penalty cannot be distributed, even among the surely guilty, in a perfect way. The poor, for instance, will almost certainly hang for their crimes more often than the rich, who can afford the brightest and best lawyers in the country. Visible minorities may also be more vulnerable in this respect, as blacks have been in those American states that have reinstated the death penalty. And those who are clearly insane-and it is these who commit some of the crimes which get the most publicity-will not be hanged in any event as the defence of not guilty by reason of insanity will continue to be available.
In recent years, Donald Marshall of Nova Scotia and John Wildman of Ontario were convicted of murder and later found to be innocent. In 1984, Senator Metzenbaum tabled in the U.S. Congress a list of 48 persons who were convicted of murder in the U.S. and later found to be innocent.
It also interesting to observe that, despite suggestions to the contrary, jurisdictions with capital punishment spend far more money than do those which have abolished such punishment. Trial and lengthy appeal costs are all borne by the taxpayer. A 1982 study showed that if the death penalty were reintroduced in the State of New York, the cost of the capital trial alone would be more than double the cost of a life term in prison.
June 25, 1987

While that is something to think about, in the final analysis,
I think we have to reject arguments for or against capital punishment based on a dollars and cents calculation. Let us be clear that the money argument cuts both ways.
The case for doing something to protect the lives of prison guards and police officers is, to many, probably the most appealing argument for capital punishment. Might I say personally that I come from a long line of big Irish cops. I am no stranger to policemen, either among my family or among my friends. My grandfather was the Chief of Police in the community which I represent here in this Parliament, and I have an uncle who has served 25 years in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I know the compelling nature of this argument, particularly for families whose members serve in these capacities.
Yet, this argument also has its limits. Prison guards are often the victims of tensions that could have been prevented through better management of the prison system; and police are often vulnerable because they are forced to work alone or under unnecessarily dangerous conditions.
Politicians who call for capital punishment but who refuse to properly finance our police departments and our prisons should not be so easily let off the hook on these issues. The question of what to do about repeat offenders who are already in prison and who already have received the maximum possible penalty under the law is a difficult one. However, that is not the motion that we have before us. I remind Hon. Members, with respect to the matter of the killing of police, that the greatest number of police killed on duty in one year was in 1962, when there were 11 police officers murdered in Canada. In that year, capital punishment existed and there were two hangings for the killing of police officers.
Since abolition in 1976, the worst years were 1984 when six police were murdered and 1985 when five police were murdered, and the number of police has doubled since 1962.
Mining is still a more dangerous profession than police work. Many miners are killed every year and many more have died over the years, not just from accidents but from diseases related to the conditions in which they work. I mention this not to make any easy or simplistic comparison between the death of a miner by accident or by neglect and the death of a policeman by gun-fire. Obviously there are significant differences. However, it raises the question of what calls for the highest degree of moral outrage.
I guess my problem is that I am just as outraged by mine owners who have knowingly endangered the lives of their employees and by factory owners who have knowingly poisoned the environment of neighbourhoods and surrounding areas. I am just as outraged by the people who allow others to die, either quickly or slowly, or to be damaged just so they can make bigger profits. These people are just as high on my list of undesirables as many of the people convicted of murder.
Capital Punishment
If we could come to see these kinds of acts as equally criminal, maybe I would not be so anxious about the fact that the present furore about capital punishment deflects and diverts us from other areas of concern. At this point we do not even prosecute, let alone punish, those who make death-dealing decisions all the time. This is not to mention, when we talk about premeditated murder, the premeditated mass murder of the entire human race which is being premeditated every day in the Pentagon, the Kremlin, and many other places around the world.
I would like to see some of the moral outrage which we get from government back-benchers about premeditated murder of individual Canadians expressed against the premeditated murder of the entire human prospect, the premeditated destruction of all creation which is being premeditated here and now, every day that we sit in the House. I would like to see some moral outrage about that for a change. I would like to see that expressed by the same people who argue that they have so much respect for their constituents' views on this issue.
I would like them to show respect for their constituents' views on that issue. The next time we have an opportunity in the House on a free vote, as we have had, to vote against the testing of the cruise missile and other death-dealing weapons, I would like to see them have the same respect for their constituents' opinions, have the same outrage as they have about premeditated murder, get up and vote against cruise missile testing. When that day comes, I will know that moral outrage has been reclaimed in a constructive, not just a destructive way.
Self-righteousness must be guarded against on all sides of the debate. Pro-capital punishment people should avoid thinking that they are the only ones who care. Those of us who are against capital punishment experience anguish and gut-rending pain when we read of children being abused and murdered. It is every bit as real for us as it is for those who are for capital punishment.
Like many people, I sometimes think what I might do if I got my hands on some of these guys, but I am still against capital punishment. It should be clearly understood that pro capital punishment people have no monopoly on the emotion which many murders generate. The debate is not about how we feel or even what as individuals we might want to do or take individual responsibility for. The debate is about the proper role of the state and society and whether there should be state directed killings.
Anti-capital punishment people should guard against the self-righteousness of pretending that they are somehow more morally advanced or civilized than those who argue for it. This is not necessarily true. Many people of goodwill feel capital punishment is a tragic necessity of life which they wish was not necessary, or they experience the cry for capital punishment as a cry for limits, for a sign that there are some things which just will not be tolerated. Even if I do not agree with it, this is understandable in a world where we are too cool by half about many life denying solutions, from nuclear war at the level of

June 25, 1987
Message from the Senate
collective morality to abortion at the level of social and individual morality.
I view it as a mistake to single out this issue as the place to reclaim moral outrage as a social good. I also regard it as a mistake or a form of self-righteousness for various small "1" liberals to pat themselves on the back for being against capital punishment, as if it is all we have to do or be to become a "civilized" society, while social, economic, and military decisions which condemn millions to suffering and death are regarded as "political realities".
Allow me, Mr. Speaker, to address the question about whether I should vote according to my own view or according to what the majority view in my riding might be, particularly if it is true that a majority might favour capital punishment. So far I have more letters of opposition to capital punishment than letters for it. I have run three times-in 1979, in 1980, and in 1984-each time against someone who wanted the return of capital punishment and who tried to make a big deal out of it. Each time I made it perfectly clear where I stood on capital punishment. I therefore believe that I can vote against capital punishment with a clear political as well as moral conscience in this regard.
I say two things to Members of Parliament here who might be feeling queasy about going against the will of their constituents in this regard. First, the will of their constituents is not as clear as they think it is. Let us look at what happens when we push someone who is in favour of capital punishment as I have.
I know many who were in favour of it, but when asked the second, the third, and the fourth question beyond just the general question, I found that they were not as in favour of it as they really sounded. Second, I ask Members to remember that because people are basically decent, they tend to respect people who are willing to put themselves on the line and to vote according to what they think is right, in spite of the fact that their constituents might disagree with them. 1 have never found that to be politically debilitating in my years in this place and in three elections.
I subscribe to the traditional Tory view of the responsibility of a Member of Parliament put forward by Edmund Burke in 1774, that a Member of Parliament owes constituents the exercise of his or her judgment and must be held accountable for that judgment at election time. He said:
Your representative owes you, not his industry alone, but his judgment, and he betrays instead of serving you if he sacrifices it to your opinion.
Surely no one would want to argue seriously although it may be tempting when one disagrees with one's Member of Parliament, that as a rule MPs should vote in mechanical obedience to the majority view in their constituencies. Such a view overlooks the fact that part of what we are paid for as
Members of Parliament is to take the time which others do not always have to study the evidence, to hear the witnesses, to read the reports, to meet the various lobby groups, to participate in the debate, to consult with our colleagues, and to vote according to our best judgment. Indeed, if Members of Parliament are only delegates doing what they are told, maybe all we need is for them to have a computer hook-up in their homes by which they can vote on everything as it comes up, without the benefit of the process which Members of Parliament now go through when they vote. I imagine that some might see this as not a bad idea, given the quality of some of the decisions we make here. However, I am not ready to declare the work I do here in Ottawa as redundant.
A final word, Mr. Speaker. This is a free vote. A free vote does not mean that we all receive the freedom to become Pontius Pilate. It does not mean that we all receive the freedom to do simply what the crowd wants, to ask the question what is truth and let the mob answer. A free vote means that we are given an opportunity, rare in this place, to exercise our own best judgment according to our conscience. That is what I hope all Members will do when it comes down to the vote, whenever that may be.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REINSTATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak in the House on the motion before us dealing with whether or not to reinstate capital punishment. I know that many Hon. Members on both sides of the House have already or will utilize this chance to express their views on this very important and highly volatile subject.
June 25, 1987

I would like to thank all those who have written to me and who have taken the time to make a concerted effort to write or talk to me on this matter. When the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) announced the motion in the House on February 13, he stated:
I would expect all Canadians to make their views known through letters, briefs or meetings ... to Members on all sides of the House.
Each of us on this side of the House may vote according to our own individual wish and not be bound by Party discipline. We appreciate this opportunity. I applaud the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who, despite his own personal opinion on the matter of capital punishment, promised this free vote and is fulfilling this promise.
In 1774, more than two centuries ago, Edmund Burke, a British MP, said:
Your representative owes you, not his industry only, but his judgement: and he betrays instead of serving you if he sacrifices it to your opinion.
He was speaking to his constituents at the time. No one here today would dare to compare himself or herself to this great philosopher, but the intention of his message is valuable to us in this debate.
When elected, a Member of Parliament's duty lies in representing the best interests of all his constituents. At the same time, we were elected for what we ourselves believed and for what we stood for. My beliefs are not a secret to my constituents.
In April 1984 when I stood for the nomination meeting for the Progressive Conservative Party in Fraser Valley East, I stated that capital punishment should be reinstated for first degree murder. My belief in that has not changed to this date.
A questionnaire that I sent to every household in my riding in December of 1984 asked this question: "Do you support capital punishment for premeditated first degree murder?" Indications were that 95 per cent of the 4,387 people who returned it voted yes.
Capital punishment is perhaps one of the most thought-provoking issues that each of us have had to face. I believe I speak for many of my colleagues when I say that I have wrestled with the pros and cons of abolishing or reinstating the penalty for some time now. I still come to the same conclusion. Capital punishment is the ultimate punishment for the ultimate crime.
Underlying all the theories which explain the purpose of criminal law is the basic premise that criminal law is the means by which society reaffirms its values and denounces its violators. These values develop to some extent in response to changing social values. Society abhors murder and anyone who intentionally, with forethought and total disregard for another individual's life, murders a person is abhorred to the same degree.
We live in a world in which at times we must make some difficult choices. The choice of reinstating capital punishment
Capital Punishment
for the crime of first degree premeditated murder is a last resort and is the choice we must make with reluctance.
Abolitionists who try to use the argument that capital punishment merely perpetuates violence are incorrect and are misleading Canadians. When a person on the street takes it into his own hands to be judge, jury and executioner and murders another person intentionally, he has denied that other person the right to be tried before an independent, impartial jury. This is murder. If society gives that murderer the right to counsel, to the safeguards inherent in our criminal law system, including an impartial, objective jury and the best legal protection and then finds him guilty without doubt of that murder, that in my opinion is justice. The difference between the two is obvious.
It is fine for those opposing capital punishment to say that no system is perfect and mistakes happen. How cavalier of them to say this and in the same breath say that we cannot have capital punishment because we may kill an innocent person.
Our laws prohibit anti-social behaviour. We must count on our criminal justice system to be objective enough to deal equally with everyone. Whatever the seriousness of the crime, the protections guaranteed by the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms apply. Maximum penalties are a statement by Parliament and thus by society that the conduct of the criminal is seriously anti-social.
It is interesting to note that the offence of murder has not changed much since 1955 when the last complete revision of the Criminal Code took place. However, its classifications and related punishments have changed. I would like to outline the changes that have occurred since 1961.
In 1961, murder was classified for the first time. Distinctions were made between capital and non-capital murder, with the former being punishable by death. The clear intent at the time was to reserve the death penalty for the most calculated and direct forms of murder. These fell into three categories: planned and deliberate, death caused by own act or otherwise directly participating in the killing and finally when the victim was a peace officer, guard or similar official, whether the murder was intentional or not. In 1961, the death sentence could be commuted to nothing less than life imprisonment.
In 1967, the Act to amend the Criminal Code changed the qualification of capital murder to apply only to those who had murdered peace officers, prison guards and similar officials who were acting in the course of their duties. Every other form was delegated to non-capital and was punishable by life imprisonment.
When this amendment expired in 1972, the law reverted to the 1961 formula. In 1974 the capital and non-capital categories were changed to murder punishable by death, reserved for those who killed peace officers and prison guards; and murder punishable by life imprisonment. This lasted three years. Capital punishment was abolished in 1976 in a narrow

June 25, 1987
Capital Punishment
vote in the House. It was at that time we adopted the categories of first and second degree murder. The difference between the two is in the sentencing. First degree murder, which includes planned and deliberate murder, contracted murder, and murder of a peace officer or prison guard, is punishable by life imprisonment without parole for 25 years. Since then there have been numerous Private Members' motions and Bills in favour of the reinstatement of the death penalty, but none have come to a free vote until now.
We must remember that this motion, if passed, will require a parliamentary committee to examine the issues relating to capital punishment and subsequently draft legislation to be debated in the House. The constitutional Act of 1867 gave the federal Government jurisdiction to legislate criminal law, with minor exceptions. This is what we are doing here today and have been doing for the past several days.
We should be careful with some of the information we have been hearing in this House from those who advocate the abolition of capital punishment. The year 1962 seems to be the time many are using to indicate that capital punishment does not deter or prevent murders. However, it is clear that year ends a period of time when little comprehensive data was kept. From 1956 to 1961 inclusive, 10 on-duty police officers were murdered. Unfortunately the data does not show how many cases were solved. However, it does show one of the killers committed suicide. Another was declared insane. Four more were convicted of murder.
It can be said, after examining the information available, that in the six years before 1962 two police killers were executed. In the supposed watershed year of 1962, 11 officers were killed out of a total of eight incidents involving 10 killers. Of those 10 persons charged, two were declared insane and the death penalty is not likely to deter those who are mentally ill. A third committed suicide and spent time in a mental institution. A fourth, who was responsible for killing three officers in B.C. in one incident, was shot and killed by police. He also had spent time in a mental institution. Four of the 10 killers who were responsible for six of the police officer murders in 1962 were mentally ill and probably would not have been deterred in any event. This information weakens the abolitionists' argument. No conclusion can be made against capital punishment as a deterrent factor for murder by using 1962 as the example.
Our society is not going to the dogs. We have not reached a stage where the call to reinstate capital punishment is the result of mass hysteria or hype. Canadians are looking at our criminal law and asking why rehabilitation is not working. Why are mass murderers such as Clifford Olson being allowed to receive special protection in the Kingston Penitentiary? Because the system fears for his life if he was incarcerated in the regular stream of a different maximum security prison. It has been reported that Mr. Olson himself, after confessing to
his crimes, said he would not have killed those innocent children if the death penalty was in effect and enforced.
Retribution means recompense for evil done. The German philosopher Kant, in the 1800s, believed that the only proper reason for punishment was the service of strict justice. The only just punishment for the unpardonable crime of murder is proportionate to that crime. Using that philosophical framework, I reiterate that with our system of criminal law, the person charged with and proven to be guilty of first degree murder, planned and deliberate or contracted, should be eligible for the maximum penalty, death.
It seems remarkable to me that the NDP, which calls for abortion on demand, turns around and righteously states that we should not reinstate capital punishment for first degree murder. The message members of the NDP are sending out is that it is all right to destroy the life of an unborn child but do not consider putting to death someone who has been convicted of intentionally murdering an innocent person. What hypocrisy.
In closing, I must say that my conscience demands that I vote in favour of this motion. I anxiously await the rest of the debate and hopefully the upcoming legislation from the parliamentary committee.

As to whether or not we should be comparing ourselves to other countries, I find in passing strange that the very Party which seems to take great delight in supporting the Socialist Soviet Union-

He asked a question and 1 will answer it. He finds that part of their law repugnant. Nevertheless, we do not base our laws on what other countries are doing. We have to shape our laws for the situation we have here in Canada.
I find it very strange that when you ask many abolitionists if there are any crimes for which they would be in favour of having capital punishment as the penalty, many of them will say, yes, if it was just for that crime. Just a few minutes ago we heard an Hon. Member say that he could see capital punishment being brought back for repeat offenders. However, he was planning to vote against the motion the way it is.
I for one want to see it brought back for a very limited number of crimes. Many people have used the argument of the sanctity of life and therefore they cannot vote for capital punishment. I, too, value the sanctity of life but the sanctity of life can be demonstrated in no better way than putting on the books the penalty for those convicted of premeditated murder. It is very difficult to prove that murder is premeditated. I do not believe there will be many people executed if capital punishment is put back on the books, but it should be on the books as a deterrent in order to save lives.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REINSTATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on two previous occasions in this House, in 1973 and again in 1976, I voted for the abolition of the death penalty. This time I decided not to rely merely on my past point of view but to rethink and reconsider my position carefully and seriously. I decided to do so to see whether there were any good and substantial reasons to justify changing my mind.
I stand for effective law and order in our society. I abhor all acts of violence and, most especially, I am repulsed and angered by violent and criminal acts against children, women, elderly people, and all other peaceful, non-violent persons who have done nothing to provoke or invite acts of terror or horror upon themselves.
I am for law and order. I believe that our police forces should be sufficiently strong in numbers and effective in the enforcement of law to prevent as much violence as possible. Our nation must have a system of justice, including punishment, which while always protecting the innocent does not allow the guilty to laugh in our faces, to be set free on technicalities or after serving only token periods of time in prison. I believe these things, especially with reference to those
Capital Punishment
who think that their problems or their way of life can be resolved or eased by way of violent acts.
During the debate on capital punishment in June of 1976 the then Prime Minister, Mr. Trudeau, said:
It is clear that the protection of innocent people against assaults on their lives and liberty is one of the highest duties of the state. It is equally clear that this duty requires the aggressive and effective prevention, prosecution and punishment of criminal violence.
It is essential that people have confidence in the law, essential that they have confidence in the ability of the legal process to protect them against the lawless.
I ask the House, however, whether reinstatement of the death penalty will help in any way to give us a better and a safer society. Will it accomplish what its advocates claim it will, that is, bring down the murder rate and make the streets safer? Will it reduce the number of violent acts in our nation?
There is a widespread belief among Canadians that a very high percentage of all crimes committed are violent. In fact, according to Statistics Canada, violent crime comprises only about 8 per cent of all crimes and homicides less than 1 per cent of all violent crime. More than one-third of all murders occur within a domestic situation in the victim's very own home. These statistics do not in any way lessen the seriousness of the problem of violence in general or murder in particular, but they do place the problem in some reasonable perspective.
It distresses me that so many who advocate the death penalty as the answer to violence in society seem, at the same time, to place so little emphasis on prevention. For example, in the constituency which I represent, there are two young people who have developed an excellent school program on violence in the home and in interpersonal relationships. Programs such as these can help so much to avoid violent acts. However, the two young people in question are experiencing great difficulty getting the funding they need to take their program to more schools and present it to a larger number of students.
Is it not curious, Sir, that if we are concerned about violence there are no resources available for a program such as this which can prevent acts of violence in the home and among those who interrelate one with the other? Dr. Nora Volkow, a Texas psychiatrist, recently told a medical conference that one-half of all violent crimes are committed by people who may have brain defects that are treatable with medicine. Murder committed by someone with a mental disorder is not culpable homicide. In the past, when the death penalty was in effect, our Criminal Code described capital murder as being planned and deliberate. Even with the death penalty, then, we do not execute sick people. Is it not entirely possible that a serious brain defect, a mental disorder of one kind or another, could go undetected and such a person could be executed?
Our system of justice is not established on the principle of vengeance. Capital punishment was generally accepted throughout the world for many centuries mainly because of the desire for vengeance as well as the recognition of the sovereign right to inflict death in the name of society. At one time many crimes were punishable by death but gradually in most western

June 25, 1987
Capital Punishment
democratic societies there came to be only one capital offence, that is, deliberate, planned homicide.
Following World War II, with its shocking record of the holocaust, its bombing of civilian populations, the use of the atomic bomb on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, there was a strong reaction throughout the western world to officially-sanctioned death. The universal declarations of human rights of 1948 recognized the rights and the dignity of man.
So, Mr. Speaker, I repeat that while our system of justice is not established on the principle of vengeance, neither is it built on the Christian ideal of turning the other cheek. Punishments are meant to be deterrents and there is no doubt in my mind that capital punishment is a deterrent. Most forms of punishment are deterrents, even fines for parking violations. Have you ever witnessed someone rushing out of a meeting in order to put another quarter in the meter?
The question then becomes whether such a drastic form of punishment as the death penalty is an effective deterrent-not whether it is a deterrent alone, but whether it is effective. Is it, for example, more effective than life imprisonment? Studies to date lead one to the conclusion that the death penalty does not have any demonstrable deterrent effect greater than that of life imprisonment. United Nations data confirm the view that abolition of the death penalty does not appreciably increase the incidence of crime.
I have heard the argument, of course, that using the death penalty is more economical than keeping people in prison. That being so, it is entirely logical to ask why not then increase the number of capital crimes and save not only a little money but a great deal. Obviously, even to pose such a question is absurd. Capital punishment can never be reintroduced on the basis of being part of any Government's program of economic restraint. In fact, executions can be extremely costly when all of the different aspects are factored in, including trials, appeals, seeking pardons and so on. At least one U.S. District Attorney has acknowledged for the record that it would be cheaper to send the killers to jail than to execute them. But then he went on to say: "But with some horrible violent crimes even if it costs more, it is worth it to put them to death". That surely is the question for this House: Is it worth it to put them to death?
Some of those who have witnessed executions think otherwise. Recently 1 took part in a panel discussion on capital punishment which was held in the City of Yellowknife. One woman there told the group that her father, an RCMP officer, once had to witness a hanging as part of his duty. He was ill for many weeks thereafter and he became a strong abolitionist as a result.
A U.S. journalist who won the draw to witness an execution said later:
Until you see it, you don't understand how gruesome it is, what tremendous responsibility it is .. . you have to block out the fact that this was a killing, not a
death. What it said was people are junk, and if you don't believe it, just watch this.
Professor Ken L. Avio of the University of Victoria in Victoria, British Columbia, in a study entitled "The Quality of Mercy: Exercise of the Royal Prerogative in Canada", has noted that those who actually did hang in Canada when capital punishment existed tended to be a limited group, more likely to be male, more likely to be an aboriginal person. Other groups which were more likely than others to die if convicted of murder were a labourer, a French Canadian, or a person whose origins were eastern European.
As well, whether clemency was granted or not depended on the number of homicides committed while one's case was being considered. If one was on death row when a number of murders took place, one would more likely hang than if one's case was being examined during a more quiescent period.
The Assembly of First Nations has written to all Members of Parliament, opposing the death penalty. The letter, signed by the National Chief, George Erasmus, says in part:
The death penalty is uncivilized, heathen, barbaric and unworthy of-a reasonable people. There is evidence all over the world that the death penalty is not an effective deterrent to the heinous offences upon which it follows. The legal system is not without failure and innocent persons have been put to death by the state.
There is further evidence that First Nations' citizens have been and are being punished by the Canadian state in disproportionate numbers and could be the most victims of a restored death penalty.
Former U.K. Speaker George Thomas, in his book Mr. Speaker tells of two murders which were committed on the same night in the Aberavon constituency at a time when Great Britain still had capital punishment. One murder was brutal, unprovoked and involved an innocent young girl. The other murder was by a young man of his girl-friend. The latter confessed and pleaded that it had been entirely accidental, having taken place on a lonely mountain road during a lovemaking encounter.
One of these young men was Roman Catholic and the other was Protestant. Both were found guilty and sentenced to death. A request for clemency was made on behalf of the young man who pleaded that an accident occurred. The British Home Secretary refused to exercise the Royal Prerogative of mercy in the one case where there was justification because he feared offending one of the two major religions in the United Kingdom. If one was Protestant and the other was Roman Catholic, then both must hang and they both did.
Speaker George Thomas writes:
When Chuter Ede left the Home Office he told the Commons that he had changed his mind about capital punishment. As I listened to him say that the case of Timothy Evans, whose innocence was proved after he had been hanged, had made him opposed to the death penalty, 1 recalled my own unhappy dealing with him and wondered if the boy from Aberavon was also on his conscience.
I have faced some criticism at home because I did not take a straw vote on capital punishment. However, one newspaper in my riding did and there was a 1 per cent return and a near split decision. I want to say that I am not opposed in any way
June 25, 1987

to a measure of direct democracy in our country. If we wish to use referendums more often, I am not against that. However, I ask Members who do not usually poll their constituents about other matters such as tax increases, free trade, or constitutional amendments why they choose the single issue of capital punishment and ask their constituents to become involved in this process?
Even if I were to take a straw vote in the constituency I represent, how valid would the results really be? A satisfactory referendum involves using full election apparatus, not merely mailing out a householder with a tear-off card which is no more than a pseudo-ballot. The results are entirely and completely inconclusive, proving nothing about the attitude of the people who live in that region or constituency.
No, I tell you that our system of democracy is to the greater degree representative in nature and it is I who must stand here in my place soon and make a decision regarding life and regarding death. It is a matter of conscience. Since I myself could never be an executioner, and since I would never want to witness a hanging which my vote, in part, may cause, I must therefore oppose the death penalty and I will vote against this motion.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REINSTATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was quite interesting listening to the Hon. Member. I respect him because he has convictions.
Does he believe that the state has a responsibility to defend the security and liberty of an individual? For instance, does the state have an obligation to defend the nation from outside invasion?
Does the Hon. Member believe that we must have armed forces that defend liberty and security of the individual? If he agrees, can he explain why he does not agree that the state has the obligation to protect the liberty and security of an individual inside the country, when the threat comes from within, whether it is terrorism or hired killers? In each instance, the state has to kill.
When there is war, the state has the obligation to defend the liberty and security of the individual. There is killing. Similarly, when someone takes an innocent life, or there is terrorism, does the state have the right to protect its citizens?

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REINSTATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is an entirely reasonable and fair question. I gather from the question that the Member was not here to listen to the first part of my speech.
In the first part of my speech I placed emphasis on the need for law and order in society, for an effective system of justice and for punishments in order that the number of violent acts could be reduced.
Then I asked the question about whether or not something as drastic as capital punishment would in fact achieve what its advocates said it would, namely a safer, better society with less violence? I used all the evidence I could muster to show that, in fact, the death penalty does not do that.
Capital Punishment
The Hon. Member asks me if I believe that we need a standing army to protect our society in the event of a war? I say of course. However, I return that question to my hon. friend and ask him: Do we go to war if we do not examine first all the other alternatives? Before we go to war do we not examine the possibility of negotiating a peace, some kind of compromise which would prevent us from a head-on conflict, death and destruction? Of course we do. We try to avoid war at all cost because we know the results are so drastic and irreversible in many instances.
I say it is the same thing within our society. Do we need something so drastic as the death penalty when there are other alternatives which are equally effective and yet do not carry all the dangers and consequences which the death penalty has upon our society?

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REINSTATEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I agree with what the Hon. Member says, but on the other hand, if we compromise to get peace at all costs, what will happen? We had this type of compromise in the 1930s. Mr. Chamberlain tried to compromise with Hitler. The result was that 30 million people were killed. So we cannot compromise on principle because we can be pushed too far. Does the Hon. Member believe there is too much of a compromise on that one point?

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REINSTATEMENT
speechtext:
The Hon. Member talks about the need to compromise to avoid war and sometimes it does not work, but surely the Hon. Member is not saying that matters ought never to be taken before the Security Council of the United Nations Organization to see whether a confrontation between two sovereign states can somehow be avoided, that somehow the United Nations can intervene and prevent war? That is a kind of compromise, a kind of peace-making operation which every Hon. Member would encourage.
I say that within our own society there are other ways of dealing with violence. We should have more programs to prevent violence in the home and among people who know each other-where most of the violence takes place, by the way- and we can have a more effective justice system to ensure that people who commit violent acts do not laugh in the face of society, thinking they can do it again and again. There are many, many alternatives before we, as the representatives of the people of this country, would have to say that we have exhausted all possibilities in dealing with crime in our society, that we have no more answers and, therefore, we must reintroduce the death penalty.
If the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) came to this House and said: "There is nothing more we can do. Nothing works. We still have violence in our society, therefore, we must use execution", then they would have a convincing case and a person like myself would have to reconsider. But I suggest to the Hon. Member and to the House that we have not exhausted all the alternatives. There is so much more we can do. We have not even begun to

seriously deal with violence in a civilized society. Until we have exhausted every single alternative, why would we turn to something as drastic, dramatic and final as the death penalty as an answer to this problem?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Government House Leader what business he intends to call for the next several days.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, again I can advise my hon. friend that, as he is aware, we have had a very productive House Leaders' meeting. We have reached agreement on the order of business for the next couple of days. Tomorrow we will begin with Bill C-60, the Copyright Act, followed by Bill C-21, the Shippers Conference Exemption Act, followed by Bill C-42, the Finance Bill, followed by Bill C-56, another Financial Institutions Bill, followed by Bill C-66, the Veterans Affairs Bill, followed by Bill C-64, the Income Tax Act and Bill C-63 the Small Business Act. If that is finished, we will go on to Bill C-70.
On Monday we will call the capital punishment debate again. On Tuesday we will call Bill C-71, that is the amendment to the Criminal Code flowing out of the Deschenes Report, Bill C-70, WHMS Bill, that is the Workmans Hazardous Materials Bill, Bill C-69, the Customs Tariff Bill.
A Bill will be introduced with respect to the farm improvement loans, I believe, tomorrow. That will be considered. It will be followed, hopefully, by Bill C-62. I understand there may be some problems with that, but if we can work those out, we would like to deal with that Bill. Then Bill C-62, which is a debt relief Bill, and Bill C-61 and Bill C-51. Bill C-61 is on proceeds from crime and we would like to move that into committee if possible, and Bill C-51, the Tobacco Bill.
It is a fairly light agenda and with co-operation, tolerance and understanding, I am sure we can get through all this and perhaps adjourn before the regular hour of ten o'clock.

subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Hon. House Leader that if tomorrow we go through Bill C-60, Bill C-21, Bill C-42, Bill C-56, Bill C-66, Bill C-64 and Bill C-70, do we understand that if they were not to be passed, they would be taking their place on Tuesday next week, or will they be eliminated and we would start next Tuesday with Bill C-71? If such was the case, I would like to know to prepare myself accordingly to speak on some of these very important Bills. Will there be a legislative committee for some? Will they be dealt with here? What exactly are we saying yes to today? I would like to know the rules.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
The Hon. Member is saying yes to nothing. I am simply outlining the order of business and it is subject to change. The details have been worked out with the House Leaders and perhaps the Hon. Member may want to consult with his House Leader.
We would hope that we would be able to dispose of those pieces of legislation. If we do not complete all the agenda I proposed for Friday, it will obviously be carried over until Tuesday. I would hope that we might be able to conclude the capital punishment debate on Monday.
